speechtext: Mr. DOHERTY moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 236, to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill relates to three matters in connection with prisons and reformatories. The first clause amends the law relating to Ontario and enables an indefinite sentence to be inflicted of not more than two years. It is most important that there should be power in the case of persons sentenced to reformatories to either shorten or extend the sentence in accordance with the condition of the prisoner, so that where a person is speedily reformed
he may be at once released and put in a position where he can establish himself as a good citizen, and in other cases that the sentence should be prolonged within reasonable limits so that reform may be effected. The principle of this has already been established, for instance, in the case of British Columbia in the Act of last session 1912, chapter 43, section 146.
The next amendment relates to the province of Prince Edward Island. In that province there is no reformatory, and this clause is" to enable the province to make an agreement with the adjoining provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick for the care and custody of offenders sentenced to a reformatory.
The next clause is the addition of part 9, which is to cover the case of a Protestant reformatory for girls which is on the point of being established jointly for the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. This legislation does not provide anything with respect to this reformatory that has not already been established with respect to the reformatories for other provinces.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
In replying to the hon.
member for Moosejaw, who referred to this some time ago, I inadvertently fell into an error. I stated that no communication with respect to the matter had been addressed to me. I found afterwards on inquiry that a day or two before, a resolution had been sent to me, and it had been transmitted at once by my secretary to the Department of Labour for inquiry as to what they knew about it, and whether there had been any investigation. On the motion of the Right Hon. R. L. Borden for Committee of Supply:

I intend to bring before this House a matter of supreme importance to this country and especially to the people of the West; that is, the present inequality of freight rates that exists as between the West and the East. I have spoken on this matter three or four times this session, and I had expected that a Bill amending the Railway Act would have been brought down and that an opportunity would there be presented of having an amendment, declaring for equality of railway rates and of other railway charges, within the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, inserted in the Act. I had also hoped that probably some of the members from the West might have made a proposition in this direction on going into supply. But, as the House is now approaching prorogation, and as the question is of supreme importance to the people of the West, I propose not only to bring the attention of the House to this condition of affairs but to ask the House to declare that it is of the opinion that there should be no discrimination as between the East and the West. I am not going into Mr. DOHERTY.
the details of the question now, for they have been presented to the House time and again. I have presented them on many occasions, and so have other members, and the journals of public opinion in the West have expressed their views, and a very prominent declaration of opinion has recently been put on record by the Board of Trade of Winnipeg.
I think I can bring the matter to the attention of the House in a very few words by saying that in my view legislation and progress are sometimes a matter ot strategy, and that inasmuch as the Canadian Pacific railway has taken advantage, as I believe, of Parliament, and advantage of the Government in increasing its capital stock as it did last year; and inasmuch as the Grand Trunk railway have been here for relief, and inasmuch as I believe there may be a proposition in connection with the Canadian Northern this session, to my mind in such opportunity Parliament should assert itself and secure from these great companies concessions in the direction of equality of railway charges in the West with the charges now imposed in the East. The Canadian Pacific railway is enormously rich; its charges are high and it can well afford to reduce them. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway wTas built for the very purpose of creating competition and reducing rates; the same policy was announced in connection with the construction of the Canadian Northern, and when we have them before us in Parliament, asking favours of one kind or another, we should demand that they should give some concessions to the people. The people of the West feel that they are not getting justice because the railway rates in the West are higher than they are in the East. Our railroads are national roads; they have been subsidized by all the people and therefore all the people should be treated equally. To my mind, even if the cost of operation were higher in the West than in the East, I would still be of the opinion that there ought to be equality of charges. These people have contributed as much in the West as they have in the East; all the proposals for relief that may go through this House will have to be made good by the people of the West together with the rest of the people of Canada. Citizenship in Canada ought to involve equality of treatment in a national proposition, and especially where the national funds are called on or have been called on to aid any proposition. If the proposition is within the jurisdiction of Parliament, if it is subsidized by Parliament, if it is relieved time after time by Parliament, then I say Parliament should say that that corporation ought to give equality of treatment to all the people of Canada. To make that clear I shall read from an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of Friday last. I am also going to read a short extract involving the declaration of

the Winnipeg Board of Trade. The Winnipeg Free Press of last Friday says:
The Free Press has all along contended that as the first step towards the remedying of the injustice of the railway rates in the west the Dominion parliament should in a formal enactment establish the principle that there must be equality in the rates in all parts of the Dominion, save and except where the railway companies show that in any section of the country there are differences of density of traffic and of costs of maintenance and operation, justifying higher rates. This applies equally, of course ,to express and telegraph rates.
I do not accept that principle of the Winnipeg Free Press that because there is density or absence of density of traffic there should be discrimination. I have already stated there should be equality of treatment, inasmuch as all the country contributes to these railways and that citizenship should involve equal treatment throughout the entire length and breadth of the Dominion. The Free Press then goes on to deal with the matter that I brought up in this House a short time ago, namely, the proposal of the Minister of Railways to increase the salary of the Chief Commis

sioner of the Railway Board. I said that I was in favour of that; but I took the opportunity of drawing the attention of the House to the inequality of railway rates. The Free Press goes on to say:
The laying down of the principle of equality would not be a complicated business at all. ft would be simplicity itself. The thing could be done in a couple of dozen words. All that would be necessary would be to draft a declaration of the principle of equality and have it incorporated in the Railway Act. The principle has been set fortb several times in the Free Press during the past few years.
It is very well set forth in the closing paragraph of the resolution recently passed by the Winnipeg Board of Trade in regard to the reported application of the Canadian Northern to the Dominion Government for further financial assistance to the extent of some $35,000,000. That resolution, after stating that the rates in the West are higher than the rates in the East, and are excessive charges for the services performed and constitute a heavy burden on the people of the West, concludes as follows:
I want to direct the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) and the members from the West to what the finding of the Winnipeg Board of Trade is in regard to this inequality of treatment:
Therefore, be it resolved that the Winnipeg Board of Trade hereby petition the Government of Canada and respectfully urge (without expressing any opinion as to whether aid should be given by the Government or not) that in the event of it being considered expedient by the Government to grant the Canadian Northern Railway Company financial aid in connection with the construction of its lines, such assistance be given only on the
346i
condition that the rates charged for the carriage of freight between points upon the Canadian Northern west of Port Arthur be reduced to an equality with rates charged by railways in Eastern Canada for similar services, except in so far and to such extent as the railway company may be able to establish higher cost of operation in the west.
That is the resolution of the Winnipeg Board of Trade. While it specifically deals with the case of the Canadian Northern railway, it asserts the principle that there should be equality. The Free Press goes on to say:
What the member for South York urged on the Miniver of Railways and the Government was simply the insertion in the Railway Act of a clause in general terms, declaring that the priniple enunciated in the closing lines of the above closing paragraph of the Winnipeg Board of Trade resolution in regard to Canadian Northern rates shall apply to all railway rates. It would be no Herculean labour to draft such a clause. There would be no need to consider a single item in a single railway rate, much less 230,000 railway rates.
I believe this resolution expresses the views of all the people of the West. The western roads have been built at smaller cost rather than at higher cost. I do not believe the cost of operation in the West is greater than in the East. If this resolution expresses the opinion of the people of the West, it ought to be put before the House, and the opinion of the House taken on this great question.
I have no faith, nor has the Winnipeg Free Press faith, in any general relief coming from the Board of Railway Commissioners. They are engaged in examining 230,000 individual tariff rates; they are taking months to do so, and they will take months more. If they do anything this year, all that they will give will be small measure of relief. Parliament ought to come to the assistance of the Railway Commission and declare that there shall be equality as between East and West. When the Board are in possession of that principle, they can easily find what fair and equitable rates should be, and then they can apply them to the whole country without discrimination. The railway policy of this country is not to be framed up by the Board of Railway Commissioners. The jurisdiction is in Parliament and Parliament ought to lay down this principle of equality in treatment. When that principle is declared by Parliament, it may be necessary for the Railway Commission slightly to increase rates in the East in order to give fair treatment to the West If that is to be done, it should be done immediately. Why should this stigma rest upon the people of the West that they must pay higher rates than the people of the East pay.? No member from the West will say that it is fair treatment for the West to be under the bondage of paying higher rates than the people of the East pay. My motion does not involve any loss of rev-

enue to the railways, but it says that the railway rates as imposed shall be e(R*ai 7 distributed as between East _ and west. Therefore it involves no unfair treatment to the railways. This principle of ity in charges applies not only to
telegraph and telephone charges but to
express charges as well as other tolls. Railway passenger rates to-day are on an equality. The maximum rate to-day by a declaration of the Railway Board is three rents 9. mile. Why not have the same thing inserted in regard to freight and all these other charges? The railways are making more money at the present time m the West than in the East. None of them are complaining of lack of business^ they are all overworked. I am not arguing for lower rates in the West; but, if it should be the case that the two weaker roads would be at a loss by a reduction of rates in the West, Parliament ought to find some means of making up the loss to these roads in order to work out this principle of equality.
I cannot put the case more clearly before the House than I have done. I have spoken about it time after time and session after session. I have been waiting to see the relief come, but it does not come. The question of freight rates has been sent to the Board of Railway Commissioners and they are probably dealing with it as best they can, but they are dealing with it without the guiding principle before them. _
We have delegated to them the question of dealing with railway matters in a large measure, but we have not delegated to them the right to frame the general policy of the Railway Act and of the Railway Commission in regard to equality of treatment. _ I trust to have the support of the entire House in this declaration of equality of treatment in connection with railways. My motion is very short. I have made no arrangements with anybody, and I do not know whether I shall get a seconder or not. I hope some member from the West will second .my motion. It is a hard thing for a member in my position to bring up a question, which has such a widespread interest, and on which there may be a wide divergence of opinion between the two parties. I beg to move:
That all the words after ' that ' be struck out, and the following substituted therefor: ' That in the opinion of this House there should he no discrimination as between Ease and West in the tolls for freight or any other service within the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.'
I shall be glad to second the motion.

I quite appreciate the courage of my hon. friend in ploughing a lonely furrow so far as his own side of the House is concerned. As he knows, I have been supposed to have done some little work in that line myself Mr. MACLEAN (S. York!
and it is not always an agreeable position. He says it is a hard thing for him to move an amendment like this in his present situation. I have always thought my hon. friend's situation was a little illogical, because he is a natural born radical. He reminds me of the "well known character of one of Moliere's plays, Jourdain, who was talking prose all his life without knowing it. I can quite appreciate that it is a hard thing for him to have come to the help of the western farmers in his own present-political Egypt. We are, as he recognizes, suffering under a disability in the West in. this matter of freight rates. I would point out that it is not the only disability under which we suffer, and I am afraid that we are -so used to being called on to make bricks without straw that- we shall cease to repine from sheer inanition if we are not stirred up occasionally by some radical like .my hon. friend. I have great hope of my hon. friend, he is a man with his eves wide open and watches the turn that political events have taken. He has good blood in him. I believe it is a, fa.ct that his father was the pioneer, from his point of view, of the protective policy in this country. He saw what they were -doing in the United States and he said: from our nearness to the United States, protection, if it is a good thing there, must be a good thing here. I am* quite sure my hon. friend has his eyes open and sees that United States are going the other way now and h-e will not be dishonourable to his father's memory if he becomes the pioneer of free trade in Canada because United States are going in that direction. I interject these remarks in the question of railway rates in order to point out that there are more kinds of bondage than one. We may be in bondage to the railway companies, but we have another kind of bondage and I want my hon. friend to give free play to his radical proclivities and show that he is a man of independence and a good Canadian, and to cross the floor of the House and join another radical like himself and then we radicals will go all abreast like the horses of the sun.	.	.
At this stage of the session I do not wish to hold up the House for any length of time, but I should say it was so plain that a wayfaring man, though a foo-l, may see the truthfulness of it, that there ought not to be any -difference between freight rates in the East and in the West, there should not be any discrimination. The way to build up a great empire is not to divide Canada whether on a naval question in the provinces or a fiscal and railway question in the provinces. The wray to get imperial unity is by means o'f Canadian unity, and if we can have Canadian unity in re-o-ard to freight rates I am sure the western

members will give my hon. friend any credit that is coming to him for having been the pioneer on the subject. I wanted to say these few words to encourage my hon. friend in the development of very hopeful symptoms which I see breaking out in him.

I wish to support the motion of my hon. friend, and give him all credit for the course which he has taken, so far as he has taken it. I think, however, he was hardly fair in giving the impression that the western members in the House had not taken due interest in this matter during this session.
I hope the hon. member will pardon me; I did not attempt to impute any such thing. I appreciate what he said -and the speeches that have been made in that direction.

In order that there may be no misunderstanding, I wanted to say that this question was brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin), and supported in the House by several other members, in the only manner in which it could be brought before the House at that time and in that condition of the business of the session. It has been a long and very strenuous session up to date; it is not possible to attend to every matter that may require attention even during the period of a very long session, and I think it will be generally agreed that at this particular stage of the session, if there is not a larger representation of western members present in the House and prepared to take part in this debate it is not to be imputed to them as blame. The western member, by reason of his distance from home, absolutely sacrifices his business during the period of the parliamentary session, whereas the member who resides in the nearer parts of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec is able, under stress, to keep up his own business at least to some extent while attending to his parliamentary duty. Therefore, the length of the session is not so material to, say, one half the members of this House who live within a twelve or fifteen-hour run by rail from Ottawa. The length of the session is not so serious to these gentlemen in the discharge of their business as it is to the gentlemen who come from the far western constituencies and particularly from the prairie west where t.heTe are just two seasons, spring and fall, and if a man is not on hand to attend to his business in the spring and fall he has not any business in the intervening season. So I say if we have not that fuller discussion of this matter that my hon. friend would like on this occasion, from western men it is a condition of circumstances that cannot be avoided. I do not wish to impute
to my hon. friend any blame. He has brought forward the matter probably as early as it was possible to bring it forward and for my own part I am entirely in sympathy with the idea of bringing it forward as a substantive motion. I am further in favour of actually voting on it. I do not wish to recriminate, but the House will remember that when my hon. friend brought a similar motion before the House at the last session it was not brought to a vote. However, there is no question about the importance of this matter to the western people and to the eastern people as well, and it is from that point of view that I wish to discuss it for a few moments.
On the great products of the West the export rates, I think, are generally admitted to be reasonable or measurably reasonable. They are special rates especially provided so as to enable the great products of the plains to be marketed profitably_ to the producer and also to the transportation interests. It is not in regard to those rates that complaint is being made at the present moment, it is in regard to the rates on merchandise and produce-on what might be called the interior rate on merchandise and produce. But as the carriage of freight under those rates consitutes a large part of the business of the railway companies and these rates give them a very _ considerable amount of revenue, the question of what those rates are to be is important both to the people and to the railway companies. Let it not be misunderstood; it is not a question of export rates on wheat or cattle that is at issue.
Except on the ocean.

It is principally the interior rates that are in question at the present time. The contention is that the interior rates in the West are higher than the interior rates in the East. On that point my hon. friend calls for a declaration of principle by Parliament. I had the honour to say, at last session of Parliament, that I believed with him that Parliament was the proper authority to make that declaration, and that it was a responsibility that Parliament had no right to lay upon the Railway Commisison. But there is this view: Does not the Railway Act as it stands to-day declare for equality of rates? Is not that the specific and fundamental principle of the Railway Act?

I think
so.

Then, if that is the fact, and I believe it to be the fact; and I certainly am aware that it was the principle that Parliament believed to have been embodied in the Act at the time it was passed -then, there has been a failure on the part of the commission, or of the Govern-

ment, or of the commission with the Government, in not seeing to it that the principles of the Act were enforced. Now, I am not going to blame either the commission or the Government because that has not been done. A certain condition did exist, and they found it in existence. Western rates were higher than eastern rates, and the Administration with the _ commission has acknowledged that condition without undertaking to remedy it; they accepted that condition and carried on under it, though it was contrary to the principle of the Act. But, I say the time has come, in my judgment, when Parliament can no longer consider that it is discharging its responsibilities to the country if it does not by declaration compel the Government -if that is the proper word-and instruct the commission as to what Parliament intends shall be done in this matter.
What should interest eastern Canada in this question of Parliament and the railway rates, and nondiscrimination in railway rates,-the (traffic that is really important in relation to the business of Canada considered as a whole-is not altogether the export rate on products from western Canada; it is not altogether the internal rate either in eastern or western Canada. May I suggest to our eastern friends that to them more especially the important question of railroad rates is the question of rates that carry the products of their industry and their merchandise to the markets of the West. Let me suggest that as the question of railroad rates of greatest interest to them. It is that feature of the railroad rates that either builds up a united Canada or breaks Canada in half.
Now, let me show my manufacturing friends and those engaged in merchandising here in eastern Canada that under existing conditions the railway company-there is only one at the present time, but we hope to have two more very shortly, though when we have two more the condition will be just the same as it is to-day, unless Parliament exercises its authority-the railway company charges transportation rates on eastern goods to western markets adjusted with a view to the railway company absorbing as large a proportion of the tariff protection as it is possible for them to do and still keep the business going. I say to the manufacturers of eastern Canada that the protection that they see in the tariff as it stands to-day is absorbed in large degree, as a matter of system and principle, by the railway company; the railway company gets it, and they do not. I hope I have been able to impress that idea upon our friends here.
They share it.

Yes, but the manufacturers think they get it all now. They do not get it all; I doubt very much if they Mr. OLIVER.
get half of it. I say it is a matter of principle, it is one of the foundation facts upon which the railway companies establish their tariffs, that they take the benefit of as much of the customs tariff as they are able, to take. And there is no way by which our friends in eastern Canada are able to protect themselves against that condition, except by the exercise of the authority of Parliament.
Is there any discrimination between the freight rate coming East and the freight rate going West for the same distance?

I could not say as to that. But my friend will understand that the rates on the great export products of the West are fixed on a special basis for export purposes, and eastern Canada has the benefit of these export rates on these great products.

It was not to the export rate that I alluded. For instance, would the rate from Toronto to Calgary on the same commodity be the same as from Calgary to Toronto? I was wondering if there was a discrimination in that.

The hon. gentleman's comparison does not hold, because the -article that is the product of Toronto is not the product of Calgary. Therefore, a tabulated rate that would show the same for the Toronto product to Calgary as for the Calgary product to Toronto would have no meaning or effect. I am taking this opportunity to state the fact, the outstanding fact, which I do not think our industrial and commercial population of eastern Canada understand, I am taking this opportunity of placing it before them strongly- that the railway company as it exists at the present time fixes its rate with a view to absorbing to the benefit of the company as large a share of the tariff protection in regard to each particular industry as it is possible for them to absorb. The result of that is that, especially in heavy manufactures or heavy goods which are produced in the United States in territory very much farther west than eastern Canada and therefore much nearer to the markets of the prairie west, these manufacturers in the United States get an advantage over the eastern manufacturer because of that adjustment of freight rates. I want that great outstanding fact to sink into the minds of our friends from eastern Canada on both sides of the House, because they may have been at some loss to know why they were hit, as they have been hit, by imports from the western states into the Canadian Northwest. That is one important and outstanding reason, and the higher the tariff is raised the higher the railroad rate will be raised. The outstanding feature that I want to keep before the House is that as

regards trade between eastern and western Canada, the tariff means tariff for the railroad, as much as for the eastern manufacturer, and probably a good deal more.
In regard to the question of the rates on railroads in the West, I would think that the question of density of population is not a factor to be considered. I would consider that cost of construction or cost of operation might fairly be considered, but I do not think that density of population should be considered. Where the population is sparse, is where there is an opportunity to build up, and in order that business and population may build up in those regions there must be reasonable Tates. To establish high rates simply gives the railroads running through unoccupied country the means of keeping that country unoccupied, which is not the intention of the constructors of the road, or the desire of anybody concerned. I do say that where there has" been excessive cost of construction, or where the cost of operation is excessive, that the railway company might reasonably be entitled to greater rates.
However, I desire to support the motion of my hon. friend because I believe it is an established fact that the foundation principle of the Railway Act as it stands to-day is not being lived up to, so far as western Canada is concerned, and without blaming the Railway Commission, without blaming the Government for that, I say that here and now is the time and place for the people of Canada to assert, direct, and give their mandate that the principle of the Railway Act in regard to equality of freight rates shall be maintained. That principle has already been established in regard to passenger rates; it is more important that it should be established in regard to freight rates, and it is upon the shoulders of the members of this House of Commons that the responsibility rests, and not upon the shoulders of the Railway Commission.

In the matter of equality of rates, there is certainly room for complaint and for a remedy, but the inequality of rates is not, I think, the only and most serious inequality. The inequality of treatment is perhaps more serious than the inequality of rates. I am not quite prepared to say that we should have uniform rates in all parts of say eastern Canada as against western Canada. In the unpopulated parts of this country it would be hardly reasonable to expect the same passenger rates as in the settled parts of the country where there are large cities. What I desire to speak of however, is the inequality of treatment, as between competing points on railways and noncompeting points. I am connected with several industries, the lumber trade
and the pulp trade, and consequently am a very heavy shipper, and my experience is, and I shall speak from experience just now, that the great grievance, is in the treatment given to shippers at non-competing points as against competing points. If we want two cars or a dozen cars to ship from a competing point, we would not have to go and ask the railway company for them. They are out catering for the business at these competing points, and there is no season in the year when they are not prepared to furnish cars on twenty-four hours' notice, or less. But at other points, where there is no competition, we can wait a month for cars. Personally I am a shipper of timber, and square timber, when ready for shipment, is almost as perishable as fruit because if left long exposed to sun and weather it becomes cracked and weather beaten, is not merchantable when it reaches the market. The only remedy we have is to say to the railway companies unless you give us cars to ship our goods you will not get any business from us at competing points. By using this threat we generally succeed in getting cars, but I do not know how it is with the poor fellow whose business is entirely at noncompeting points. I think that this is a question that the Government of this country should take up and deal with. There does not seem to me to be any reason why a railway company can supply cars on twenty-four hours' notice at competing points, and cannot supply them at noncompeting points within a reasonable time. This is a point which my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) has not touched upon, but it is a condition from which the public are suffering more than from the inequality of rates. For my part, I would quickly pay one or two cents additional per hundred if I could get a car when I wanted it in preference to having goods damaged by delay in for cars. When goods are not merchantable when they reach the market, it becomes a serious question.
Mr. J. D. TAYLOR (New Westminster). It is one of the advantages of a periodical change of Government that translation from right to left in this House brightens the minds of so many hon. gentlemen and makes them conscious of long outstanding facts of which, for a long period, they appear to have been utterly unconscious. I am delighted indeed to hear a member of the late Government (Mr. Oliver) champion equality of treatment between East and West. I am all the more delighted to hear it because it has always seemed to me strange that any western minister, like him, should have been content to rest so long in control of the administration of affairs, particularly with regard to the West, and to pay no attention to the representations made to

him and to his colleagues in the Government for equal treatment.
With respect to the amendment now before the House, I may say that it was not because of any lack of sympathy with the suggestion that the hon. gentleman who has moved it found that he was ploughing a lonely furrow. He would have had no difficulty at all in securing a seconder, or supporters for a resolution of this kind, if it. had been made at a time^ when it seemed to be with serious intent, instead of for the purpose of advertising. This is no new thunder which has been sprung upon the House to-day. This matter of the equalization of rates, and the securing of justice to shippers to and from the West, so far from not having received attention, has been receiving the most elaborate attention and is now before the Railway Commission, it having been presented in a most thorough way through the efforts of the boards of trade of British Columbia, in co-operation, I believe, with the boards of trade in various parts of the prairie provinces. We have strong hopes of success in our efforts before the Railway Commission, because we believe that if the Railway Commission find that the representations which we have made to them in an orderly and regular manner are justified, and that they lack the power to make such order as they desire to make, they will apply to Parliament in an authoritative way and ask Parliament for the necessary power. If they do, I am in strong hopes that such a request shall receive the support of hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House.
The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has been rather careless in his concluding statement to the House, that passenger rates have already been equalized. If he had given the attention to the subject which anyone who was earnestly interested in the success of this movement might have been expected to give, he would have known that on the contrary passenger Tates have not been equalized, but that the province of British Columbia suffers still from a disability to which it was subjected very many years ago, and that the railways are permitted to charge, and do charge, the extortionate rate of five cents per mile in British Columbia, whilst in eastern Canada the rate is three cents per mile. I would press upon the attention of the Government the advisability of removing the permission which the railway companies have to make that discrimination; and, further, the advisability of dealing with the subject of American railroads crossing the border into our Dominion and taking advantage of the Canadian law to charge in Canada rates which are double those charged on contiguous portions of their lines in the United States. I have in mind particularly the Great Northern Tailway line from Mr. TAYLOR.	'
Seattle to Vancouver, running for about twenty miles through the district that I represent. The company charges the full five cents per mile on the -Canadian side of the border as against two cents per mile on the American side, notwithstanding the fact that the traffic is quite as great in Canada as it is in the United States, and notwithstanding the fact that the railway has no justification at all for this increase in the charge, except that the Canadian law permits it, and it takes full advantage of the law without any other reason whatever. I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that these abuses do exist, and I would suggest to him that this matter might very well be made the subject of serious consideration at the first opportunity on which Parliament can consider it. While we do not expect a change of this kind to be made as an amendment to Supply, we from the West are strongly in sympathy with the principle's laid down by the mover of this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, before we leave this subject, I have just one or two words to -say. First of all, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Taylor) has not in my judgment added very much to the case that has been made out in reference to the question that is before us for consideration. I do not think that I ever heard the hon. member for New Westminster rise to address this House that the chief substance of his argument was not this: You did not do it; why should you expect us to do it? The hon. gentleman says that this is no new question that is before us. The hon. gentleman is right; it is not -a new question; it is not any newer than the oriental question in which m-y hon. friend was so interested when he sat on this side of the House, instead of where he sits at the present time. The railway question and the oriental question were questions upon which the hon. gentleman raised his voice very frequently in this House, but with reference to the oriental question the hon. gentleman has not -a word to say. Perhaps -it is too much to expect to hear from the hon. gentleman on that question now. Probably his voice gave out when a change of administration took place. His views changed with the change of position that his party made in this House.
With reference to the- question brought up by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), hon. gentlemen know perfectly well that the question is one of vital interest to the people of western Canada and to the people of Canada at large because that which affects the welfare of the West certainly affects the welfare of the East. If we are discriminated against, if the railways are taking away the prosperity of

the people of the West, it is going to reflect very greatly upon the welfare of the manufacturing and other interests in eastern Canada. I am still of the opinion that the proper tribunal to deal with this question is the Board of Railway Commissioners. It is before them at the present time.
I think that the present railway legislation does not give that board authority to deal with this question. If it does not give them that authority, then I agree with the hon. gentleman that it is the duty of this Parliament to give them the necessary power. I do not think it would be in the best interests of the House and the country that we should undertake the expert investigation necessary to determine the truth of this matter, the grounds upon which railways discriminate as between one part of the country and another. It is a matter for expert investigation. I have faith and confidence that if it is demonstrated that there is unfair discrimination in the freight rates as between the East and the West the Board of Railway Commissioners will deal with the matter in a way that will be satisfactory.
My complaint against the present Admin- istration is' that, as this matter has been referred to in this House before, they are not forcing the case forward for the consideration of the commission in the way they ought to. It has been discussed already and I do not propose to go over the same ground, but I do submit that if this Government were as anxious to see this ease determined as they ought to be in the interest of the public, they would see that this now almost interminable delay in dealing with the question by the Railway Commissioners does not exist any longer. The hon. member for New Westminster speaks of the discrimination in passenger rates as between British Columbia and the rest of Canada. My hon, friend knows very well that about three years ago 'the McBride Government came into office as the result of a contract between them and the Canadian Northern Company. I wonder if the McBride Government, as political friends of my hon. friend, took precautions, when they were making that contract, to safeguard the rights and interests of the people both as concerning freight and passenger rates in that province. There is no question of doubt that the McBride Government have had their share of responsibility if there is a discrimination in that province as to passenger rates in British Columbia as compared with other provinces.
The hon. gentleman also complains of the fact that the American roads running into Canada charge a higher rate in Canada than they do in the United States. Of course they do. When they cross the boundary they are not under American law, and certainly if the Canadian railways are compelled to reduce their passenger rates the American roads in Canada will be compelled to do the same. I see no point in referring particularly to the American railroads and the differences in their charges in Canada as compared with their charges in the United States, because any change in tariff that is brought to bear on the Canadian railways, will affect the American roads operating in Canada.
Our Canadian roads to-day are carrying people in Michigan, and other American states for two cents a mile while they are charging Canadians three cents a mile in Canada.

I am quite aware of that fact, and I agree that if they can carry for two cents in the United States their rates in Canada are too high. The population is I believe denser in the states referred to by my hon. friend than in western Canada. I am not defending the tariffs in Canada on any of the railways, hut 1 am simply pointing out in reference to the argument of the hon. gentleman from New Westminster that if the tariffs on the Canadian roads are altered, that will necessarily affect American railroads operating lines in Canada. This is a live question and my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) deserves the support of tne House in the object he has in view, namely, the lowering of freight and passenger tariffs in Canada and the bringing about of equality between one part of Canada and the other. But I still hold the opinion I have always held, that the proper tribunal to settle the question is the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, within whose sphere it lies. If there is responsibility, that responsibility lies with the Government and with the Minister of Railways particularly to see that the dilly-dallying that has occurred up to the present on the part of counsel, representing the Government and the public before the commission, shall not be permitted to continue and to cause further delay. I trust that the Minister of Railways will see that his counsel will be asked to bring this matter to a speedy and, we trust, successful conclusion.

I am a little surprised that I
got no notice of this motion. I was attending a meeting of the Railway Committee, considering some Bills that had been referred to us by the Senate, when this motion was made in the House, and I did not have an opportunity of listening to the remarks of the mover or of the seconder, and I only heard part of the address of the hon. member for Edmonton.
I can look upon this motion as nothing but a vote of want of confidence, not only in the Government, but in the Railway Commission. The rate question was dis-

cussed here nearly one whole day by gentlemen on both sides, and I then took the ground that there had not been any dillydallying or delay on the part of the commission. This is a bigger task to undertake than any of the members of this House realize. The chief commissioner told me that there are in the West 230,000 different tariff rates. We have an expert working on these rates, and we hope very shortly that the commission will be able to determine the matter and announce their finding. If there is not authority in the Act, then I agree with the member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) that we should put it in the Act. The commission is the proper place to decide this case; they have the expert officials competent to study out these things and decide the matter on the principle of justice.
As to the statement of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor), I certainly will bring that to the notice of the Government and make inquiry with respect to it, because I do not think the American railroads which come into this country should charge higher rates than they do in the United States.
One remark made by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) was, I think not quite fair, when he said that through sparsely settled country rates should be as low as thickly settled country, because it cost the same amount anyway to run the trains. I think he is a little wide of the mark there. I cannot accept the resolution.

The Railway Commission
has made certain reductions in express rates; did they reduce these express rates so that the rates in western Canada should be equal to the rates in eastern Canada?

I understand they
have not reduced the rates in the East at all. They found that in the East the expenses are going up and the receipts coming down. The experience of the parcel post system in the United States is that it has reduced the receipts of express companies by twenty-five per cent in less than six months, and when the Parcel Post Bill of the Postmaster General is passed, the same result may probably follow here. It was felt that the rates could not be lower in the East than they are today. I cannot tell what a comparison of the eastern and western freight rates would disclose, but I understand there was a reduction of twenty per cent in many instances Tvest of lake Superior.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Any differences over
last year are due to increases and some promotions under the Civil Service Act.
There is an increase in the number of employees. Will the hon. minister explain that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are six in
the first division, sub-division B. That is the result, I think, of one promotion from one division to another. The first division, sub-division B, is where the increase is to be found. This is to provide additional clerical service particularly or entirely of stenographers and persons doing that class of work.
What salary does Mr. Beauchesne receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
His salary is fixed in
the supplementary estimates at $2,800. He came in originally, temporarily, to do work in connection with pecuniary claims, and was paid $200 a month. His services have been found perfectly satisfactory.

Mr. Beauchesne is a
personal friend of mine and a confrere of the Bar of Montreal. If he were to confine his activities to the Justice Department, he has every reason to aspire to the higher ranks of the Civil Service. But, speaking frankly, I am informed that he does other work, work of a political nature. He is an excellent writer, as my hon. friend knows, and I am told that he is writing for the Conservative press and in the interest of his party. I do not know whether that is true or not. I am glad to see him in the Department of Justice and hope he will remain in the department and give his time to the work there. I make no charge against him, but simply say what I have heard, not with the intention of injuring him in any way. He has great ability and wide knowledge, especially of the law of the province of Quebec, and can be of great usefulness to the department. He is an excellent writer, as I have just said, as good a writer as he is a lawyer; but I hope he will give his time to the work of the department. I would be pleased to see him advanced to higher ranks in the department; but he must not be there to do political work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of his doing work outside of the department or of doing work of the kind the hon. gentleman mentions. However, from what I know from personal observation, as well as from reports presented to me by the deputy minister and the assistant deputy, Mr. Beauchesne is most diligent, and the work he does fully justifies the enconiums upon his abilty and knowledge of the law which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) has given voice to. It certainly is to be expected that a gentleman in his position would devote his time to the service of the 1 department, and the results of Mr. Beau-

chesne's work would seem to indicate that he does so. I have no knowledge of his engaging in any other occupation.

Will the minister kindly give the names of the employees in the first division, sub-division A? The heading on twelve made ' The Department of Justice including the penitentiary branch,' I would like to know whether this includes the inspectors of penitentiaries. If so, I have some observations to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the first division, sub-division A, includes the inspectors of penitentiaries.

This would include the
salaries of Mr. Douglas Stewart and Mr. G. W. Dawson. And I understand that a new inspector has been appointed, Mr. Hughes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are only tw'o inspectors, Mr. Stewart and Mr. Hughes. Mr. Dawson has recently been transferred to the Department of Public Works.

I would repeat a suggestion that was talked over last session a good many times, that there should be an inspector familiar with the French language. My hon. friend is aware there are in the penitentiaries nearly two thousand convicts. There are nearly five hundred resident convicts in St. Vincent de Paul in my own riding, and I feel pretty sure that seventy-five per cent, certainly sixty per cent, of the convicts and also of the guards and other employees are not familiar with the English language at all. I know that inspectors Stewart and Dawson have sometimes great difficulty in cases that arise, and have had to employ the services of an interpreter. It seems to me that that is a very queer position. Disciplinary offences will sometimes cause severe punishment. The inspector is to decide and impose the punishment, and it may be a punishment of two, three, four, and even, six months. I have received complaints on the part of convicts, and on the part of guards that they could not express themselves fluently in English, and some could not speak English at all, and the judgments delivered by the inspectors were sometimes not to the point. I would say-and I think in this I wall be supported by the majority in 'this House-that, if not a French-Cana-dian, which I would prefer, at least a man .Should be 'appointed in itbe inspection department who is familiar with .both languages.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think a great deal is to be said in favo'ur of the hon. gentleman's suggestion. I may be allowed to say Ithat the existing state of affairs I inherited from the Government which the hon. gentleman supported, which had two inspectors neither of whom spoke French. The hon.
Mr. DOHERTY.
gentleman says that complaints have been made arising out of this condition. If complaint is made of injustice done through failure of the inspectors to understand French, or from any other cause, I should be pleased to have these cases brought to my notice and will do my best to reetifv them. I realize the importance of what the hon. gentleman says of having^ an inspector or some similar officer qualified in the respect he mentions. I confess, I took the situation as I found it, and it did not occur to me to make a change. But now. that he has brought it to my attention, I shall be .pleased to consider to what extent it will be possible, for me, under the circumstances, to meet his suggestion.

If I may be allowed to make another suggestion, it would be that the work of the inspectors is too great. It must not be forgotten that there are seven penitentiaries, and the inspector has to travel from New Westminster to Dorchester. I should favour the appointment of an inspector for each penitentiary, but, if thait cannot be done, at least the number should be increased. Then it would be possible to appoint a man familiar with the French language, and I know his services would be appreciated and would be for the benefit of the administration of justice, for there are many convicts _'in every penitentiary who are more familiar with French than with any cither language.

I think the suggestion
of the hon. member for Laval is deserving of consideration. My own opinion is that, instead of there being two inspectors, there should be three: and if there were three, I think his contention would be quite reasonable, that one of the three should be a man conversant with the French language. It often happens that in the administration of the penitentiaries it is found necessary for one of the inspectors to take the place of the warden for the time being. It requires no argument that, in the case of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, if this action were necessary the man to_ temporarily relieve the warden of that institution should be thoroughly conversant with the French language. I think the position taken is a very reasonable one, and while I would not like to see the number of English-speaking inspectors reduced, because most of the institutions are what might be called English-speaking, I think an additional inspector should be appointed, one thoroughly conversant with the French language.
Under what circumstances was Inspector Daw'son transferred to the Public Works Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The transfer was made because the qualifications which he possesses, a knowledge of building operations

and things of that kind, qualified him particularly to be of greater usefulness in that department than in the particular department in which he was, although I am not reflecting in the slightest degree upon the performance of his duties as Inspector Dawson.
