At the opening of the
session, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), in seconding the Address, made quite a few remarks about penitentiaries; and, if you will permit me, Mr. Chairman, without referring to a previous debate, I would like to quote a few of his remarks. They were made in good faith and with the intention of improving our penitentiary system-there is no doubt about that. But I will have to take exception to a couple of his observations. He says:
I would like to take advantage of this opportunity, Sir, to urge on the Ministry the necessity of doing something that will make the men in these institutions better fit when they leave them to earn their living.
I quite agree with the hon. gentleman on this point.
On a Sunday afternoon I have spoken in the Kingston penitentiary to 600 men whose faces showed nothing but sullen despair and hopeless sorrow.
I would like to have an explanation as to whether this was an infringement of I the rule. I have never thought of going

to the penitentiary of St. Vincent de Paul and addressing a meeting there. I do not know whether my hon. friend means that he went there to pay a visit, in which he would have been within his rights, as it is a privilege that every judge and every member of this House has. I hope the hon. gentleman will tell us what was the purpose of his meeting. We read in the papers the other day that Sarah Bernhardt visited the penitentiary at St. Quentin in California and gave a grand performance before the convicts. There was an address presented to her by a convict who had been born in France. I presume that this was done from a humanitarian point of view and in the expectation that it might improve the condition of the convicts. But I would like to know what kind of a speech my hon. friend made at Kingston penitentiary-whether it was on religion, humanitarian, or political lines.
I believe that something can be done to improve the condition of these men.

They are not voters, are
they?
No, but they might become voters after they had served their terms.
You could not be sure of it if it were a close election in Manitoba.

The Grits brought them out of the asylum to vote against me.
Mr. WILSON (reading) *
I believe that something can be done to improve the conditions of these men, and 1 want to urge upon the Minister of Justice, whose humanitarian principles I well know-
As we all do.
-and on the Minister of Agriculture, who will I know recognize the necessity in this matter, that such steps be taken as will make each penitentiary a demonstrative and reformative institution. There is no reason why cheap land should not be bought and be so developed that the farmers who live in the adjacent municipalities and districts may come and see what is being done, and how they may best improve their own condition. In following ont these principles a favour will he conferred upon the prisoner, because when he leaves the penitentiary he will not, be obliged to enter again the city slum with all its temptations, and a Tavour will be conferred on the agricultural classes, because from one end of this country to the other the cry goes up for farm help. A favour will likewise be conferred on tne state by freeing it from what must always he a burdensome load.
I do not know if there is any farm attached to the penitentiary at Kingston, or to any other penitentiary, except St. Vincent de Paul, where I know there is one. The penitentiary farm is between three
hundred and four hundred acres in extent; it has a quarry on it, a large stone bam and also a wooden barn. I know something about farming, because, like most of the members of this House, I was brought up on a farm, and I think it is my duty to say that the worst farming done in Canada is on a penitentiary farm. It has been so in the past under every Government, it is so now, it will continue to be so, and it cannot be otherwise. It is all very well to call for an eight-hour day, and that is the rule applied at the penitentiary, but you cannot apply it to farming work and be successful. If the diligent farmer wakes at four o'clock in the morning he sees the sun rise; he knows more than science about the condition of the weather; he will -wake up his sons or employees and get to work to save the crop, and he will work during the day continuously until the storm comes. That is not the way in the penitentiary; the convicts rise at half-past six in the morning; they go out to the fields to work, at 8 a.m., and at half-past eleven they line up and come into the penitentiary for lunch; they return at one o'clock and come back at four or half-past four so as to get to their cells at five o'clock. How could you run a farm on such principles ? I suggest that we should sell the land around the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, retaining only a few acres on which to grow the table vegetables which are used in the institution.
I presume the same , conditions obtain at other penitentiary farms as at St. Vincent de Paul. Therefore, instead of favouring' the proposition of my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), which has been made in good faith and for a good purpose, I would urge the minister to get rid of some of the land around the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. That land has increased	in	value enormously.Land around Montreal that was worth fifty dollars	an	acre	some years
ago, is now worth $2,000 an acre and I would not be surprised if the minister could get $500 or perhaps $1,000 an acre for the St. Vincent de Paul farm which money could be used to much better advantage than at present. Indeed, the Department of Agriculture could establish an experimental farm there, but not to be cultivated by convicts, who are limited to working at certain hours.
Then again, the farm superintendent at St. Vincent de Paul has great trouble in finding men to work the farm, because it is only short term men who are allowed outside the walls of the penitentiary, and sometimes he runs short of labour. I have seen very excellent crops of hay and oats lying on the field in the penitentiary farm without sufficient labour to save them,

people around; and, although it may be a good warning to them, on the other hand I think the convict's life is not so gay that the Government should make it more unpleasant. I think a couple of men at reasonable salaries could do all the work that is required, and the convicts could earn something for the benefit of the department by working within the precincts of the penitentiary. They have their own private road to the farm. I have even seen ladies taking the back streets so as not to meet convicts who will look at them sometimes in a very queer way. Real estate values at St. Vincent de Paul are not so high as in other villages on account of being within the shade of the penitentiary.
I have practiced mostly before the criminal courts for the last eighteen years, and have often heard judges make this remark: Young man, I do not know what to do with you; you are only sixteen, seventeen, or eighteen years of age. I pity the condition of that poor man. I should like to see the time when no young man under 21 years of age should he sent to the peniltent'iary. But our judges believe-and under the circumstances we cannot say that they are wrong-that it is beitter to send a man to the peniteniary for two years than to send him for twenty-three months to the common jail. This was more especially true in Montreal until the Bordeaux prison was completed. The lion. Minister of Justice knows the awful condition the prisoners were in in our city jails, and it is no wonder that the judges should prefer to send the prisoner to Sit. Vincent de Paul. I think that the aim of 'the penitentiary is fausse. The men sentenced to penitentiaries are supposed to be sent there to learn a trade-a man would be sent to the carpenter shop if he desired it, and if there was room, or to the shoemaker shop, or be taught some other trade. It seems to me that a wrong idea has been dominant in our penitentiaries for the last Itwenty years at least, and possibly ever since Confederation, and that is the idea that the penitentiary should benefit i'ts'elf from the work of the convict. And this is the reason for the amazingly small product of the penitentiary works. From what I have seen at St. Vincent de Paul, or Kingston or any other penitentiary, I do not believe that our present system turns out good tradesmen. There is a hospital to be built, a warden's house Ito he built, a north wing to be built, a wall to be built, and word constantly coming from the department that the work is to be rushed. The guards do not take the trouble to teach a man the trade properly- they cannot do it under Sthe system. When a man at 17 years of age is put to learn the trade of stonecutter, let us say, he should be under instruction, and if the 347
stone is not properly cut, let him begin over again, as at school. But that is not the system. The work has ko be done, whether it is done well or not, because the primary idea is that the whole work should be done by the convicts. Thak may save money to the country, but now that we are trying to improve the convicks, I do not think the saving to the country is of such importance. I make these suggestions in good faikh.
So far as the staff is concerned, and so far as the officials of the Department of Justice are' concerned, with regard to penitentiaries, I do nok think there is much fault to be found. So far as I have come in contact with the employees of the penitentiaries, I have found kbem anxious to do their work well, ready to take suggestions, even inviting suggestions, and putting them in practice to improve conditions. I say this not to pay them compliments, but merely to give them what belongs ko them. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) four ydhrs ago spoke in the same way on similar occasion, declaring that in St. Vincent de Paul, for instance, there was practically no room for improvement under our present sys'tem. I have_no doubt that the Minister of Justice, who has done well, will give my suggestions his best consideration, and will carry them out if they are good.

The hon. member for Laval (Mr. Wilson) has asked me how it came that I delivered the address to the convicts in Kingston penitentiary to which I made reference in the early part of the present session. It has been the custom for some years in the penitentiary for the chaplain from time to time to invite those whom he thinks interested in penitentiary work to address the convicts on Sunday afternoons in relation to any non-controversial subject. It was in relation to such a subject that I addressed the men that afternoon. If my memory serves me correctly the general theme of that address was 'The "opportunities of the unfortunate.' I can understand that my hon. friend would not be in a position to appreciate that subject in its fullness, and therefore I shall not go into details. But I can assure him that if he will come to Kingston any Sunday afternoon, I shall be glad to spend an hour listening to him, and if he will-

Will the hon.
gentleman provide me a seat between two convicts?

I will provide him with
that wrhich I am sure he would like, a seat on the platform. In relation to the work of the penitentiary my hon. friend and I differ radically as to the way in which the



convicts should be treated. He seems to think that the penitentiary farms should be managed from the point of view of saving to the state. I take the exactly opposite view. I think the penitentiary farms should be so managed as to give a maximum of education to the convicts so that they may leave these institutions better able to do a useful life's work. I believe that the objects of the penitentiary are reformative as well as punitive, and I think that in the administration of our institutions we have emphasized too much the punitive idea and have lost sight almost altogether of the reformative. I believe farm work can be so conducted that there will Ibe little or no loss to' the state and a distinct gain and advantage to the convicts.
We have heard not a little during the present session about the cost of living in Canada. Go back to fundamentals and you will find that the reason the cost of living is increasing is that industrial occupations are taking the men out of the country, and the proportion of men and women engaged in industry is now much greater in proportion to the total population that it was a few years ago. In other words, the farming population is proportionately growing less, while the demand of the inhabitants of cities, towns and villages for our natural products is growing greater. You cannot make two eggs do the work of four, you cannot make twice the beef from one animal that you made from two before. The demand for these natural products is increasing more rapidly than the supply. What does that mean? It means that the greatest opportunity for the convict is to go back to the land; that he should be removed for his own good from the city conditions and for the advantage 'of the country put back upon the land where his work is most in demand. For that reason, if the minister could be induced to develop this farm-work side of penitentiary life, he would be conferring a favour upon the state and upon the convict as well. I do not know about the penitentiary in the province of Quebec. From what little knowledge I have of farm conditions in Ontario, and from what I have observed while driving around, I should say that the penitentiary farm in Kingston is well run.
What is the area?
I am told by the inspector that it is some three hundred acres. The education given on that farm has certainly redounded to the advantage of the country.

At what hour in the afternoon do the convicts leave the farm work?
Mr. NICKLE.

It depends on the season of the year; in summer, about 5.30, in time to have the penitentiary locked up at six o'clock. No disadvantages will redound from the men being given farm work. It is a very simple, practical thing.
Contractors tell me that when the ordinary penitentiary convict is liberated and goes to them for work he shows by his colour and bv the state of his muscles that he has been a convict, that he is not a physically fit man, and as a result they do not care to employ him at an ordinary rate .of wage. I believe that if those men could be put out in the open and given stiff manual labour their skin would become tanned and their muscles hardened and they would be able for a day's work when they left the penitentiary. I quite agree with the >hon. member for Laval that it is objectionable that convicts should have to meet from time to time the public under disadvantageous circumstances. I would direct as I have done in private the attention of the minister to what I consider a most unfortunate practice, that of having the liberated convicts accompanied to the railway station by uniformed guards.
That is correct.

When a man has served his time in the penitentiary, the moment he leaves the gate of the penitentiary he should be a free man and I object to any system that authorizes a keeper in uniform to accompany him to the station so that every man on the train knows that a convict is on the train with him.

My hon. friend
knows that this practice is followed because in some cases when men have been (liberated from the penitentiary and have been supplied -with tickets to the places from which they came, they have gone to the corner hotel, sold their tickets and gone on a spree and perhaps have come hack to the penitentiary that night and brought something in the way of * square face ' for the other convicts.

My hon. _ friend misses
my point. I was not objecting to the prisoners being accompanied to the train by a guard but by a uniformed guard so they may be recognized as convicts. In relation to the question of trades, if one examines the returns as shown in the report of the Minister of Justice, one cannot but be struck with the number of young men who are serving first terms in the penitentiary. I am tofd that the instruction given in the penitentiary is not of such a character as to be of very great practical value when the inmate leaves the institution. The labour is direct manual labour of the old school type and does not equip them for taking their place in life in relation to

modern methods where intricate and involved machinery is used and, with the hon. member for Laval, I hope that some solution may be devised by which a better opportunity will be afforded the convicts of acquiring a trade. I quite realize that it is unwise and impossible to britag' into competition with the free labour of the outside world, the product! of the' manufactories of the peniten-t tiary. There certainly must be a loss to the state, but the loss which the state suffers through instruction in trades being imparted to the inmates of the penitentiary would surely be more than overborne by the benefit through the men being able to earn a living when they are freed from the institution.
Has that not been done in the past?

No. There is one piece of road which has been maintained for a number of years by convict labour, but there are other pieces of road which I think should be maintained in the same way. I would not restrict the application of this principle to penitentiary farms. It should be applied also to military property, and I am pleased to say that the late Government did take a piece of road in the vicinity of Kingston under their control and maintenance. I think the same principle should be applied to the roads in the vicinity of these large institutions. Every person in the province of Ontario, and I presume also in the province of Quebec, knows that the principal tax on the people is the school tax. The second largest tax is probably the road tax. Of course these properties contribute nothing to either of those taxes, and necessarily the burden is proportionately increased in that neighbourhood. It is right that we should have, and we do have, a certain amount of sympathy with the convict. I think that when the convict is released,	the	guard	who takes	him tothe station,	and	places	him on board the* train, should go in civilian clothes, and not	in"	the	regular	guard'suniform. I	think that is a goodsuggestion, and one which could be easily carried out. I do not see anything that could be said against it. But there is another class of people who are affected by the incarceration of a certain element of the population, and who are more entitled to our sympathy than the convicts. I think we would be perfectly justified in placing convicts	at remunerative	labour,
and in placing a value upon their labour. I think it would have a very beneficial effect if part of the money so earned by the convict were applied for the benefit of that convict's family, who, under our system, are obliged to suffer for the sins of * the person who is convicted. A man is sent to the penitentiary, he may be the head of a family, and the children are obliged to suffer for his misdeeds. It is not fair, I do not know that I could outline just what plan should be adopted, but it occurs to me that a value might be placed on the convict's labour, as it is placed upon his labour in certain lines, and it might be held out to him as an inducement to good conduct that a portion of the money so earned would be applied for the benefit of his family who, under the present system, are made to suffer through no act of their own.
It is not my intention to go into details in regard to the running of penitentiaries at the present time. But I do not believe there is a proper division of labour amongst Mr. EDWARDS.
the guards in the. penitentiary. I think some men have to work longer than others and do not get just as fair a show as some others receive. I think the guards are entitled to the increase which is being given to them this year. The cost of living has increased for them, as it has for other people, and their work is of such a kind that they are in more or less danger. If they perform their work properly, they are running risks which should call for a higher remuneration than they have received in the past. There are one or two cases which I hope the Minister of Justice will consider in connection with the Kingston penitentiary in the past. I have in mind one [DOT] man of whom I spoke to the minister some time ago. He was for many years a guard in the Kingston institution, and there was not the slightest black mark against his conduct, which was all and everything that should be. Through an accident he lost the sight of one eye, but he was still retained.
Did the accident happen when he was discharging his duties?

The accident occurred while he was engaged in his duties as a guard in that institution. The man's name is Charles MeConville, who has a very long record as a very efficient guard in that institution. He lost the sight of that eye through the neglect or the inability of the surgeon of the penitentiary at that time. He was, however, retained in his position as guard notwithstanding that he was there against the regulations of the institution, being a man with only one eye. He was advised by some of his friends to say nothing about it. Some time after this accident happened a convict escaped. A number of convicts wrere down at the wharf and one escaped for a few hours. That was made the excuse for the dismissal of this man, MeConville. He was dismissed when Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper was Minister of Justice. The action of the Minister of Justice at that time does not reflect anything to his credit. He used that man with extreme harshness.
I am bringing the case before the House in order to emphasize what I have said privately to the Minister of Justice that this case should be looked into. That man, after serving something like twenty-five years, without a single mark against him in all that time, was dismissed without any gratuity or recognition.
We have seen worse than that lately.

If you have seen worse oases than that then those cases should be considered. What is -the use of talking about administering justice if you pass over a case of that kind and not grant

justice to a man who is entitled to be fairly treated and has not been fairly treated ? I do not care who is responsible, that man's ill-treatment in the past should be rectified at the earliest possible opportunity.
This morning I took occasion to back up a suggestion made by the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Wilson) with regard to the appointment of another inspector who had a knowledge of the French language. I think that suggestion is a good one. Very frequently we have had to send inspectors to an institution to take charge of it for a time. We have had very efficient men as inspectors; especially is this true of the oldest inspector in the service, Mr. Stewart, who knows every detail of penitentiary work. But there are occasions when, as I have said, an inspector may go and take charge, and I think that there is such an occasion at the present time in connection with the Portsmouth penitentiary. The present warden, Col. Irvine, who" is a very efficient man, is temporarily absent on account of illness and I do not think it is right that that institution should be in charge of a man against whom charges have been made for misconduct in his official capacity. I think that some person should be sent down there to take charge of that institution until such time as the charges against this official have been investigated as they should be investigated.
Did my hon. friend say that there were charges against Colonel Irvine ?
No, I did not.
What charges does the hon. gentleman refer to-I did not catch what he said.

I said that I did not think it was just the correct thing to have that institution in charge of a man against whom charges had been made. I do not cast any reflection upon Colonel Irvine at all, because I believe he is a very efficient man. But it does occur to me that this is an occasion when one of the inspectors of the penitentiary should temporarily take charge during the illness of the warden, and especially in view of the fact that charges nave been laid against a person who, in the absence of Colonel Irvine, is the head of the institution. There are many particulars in which Portsmouth penitentiary will compare very favourably with any of the other penitentiaries in various parts of the Dominion. Stoney Mountain was not capable of holding some desperadoes and they were senH, down to Kingston. It was a difficult matter to hold them there, they made a break for liberty, but were recaptured. I think that the
Kingston penitentiary in that respect has a very enviable record. The officials have been very alert and have shown themselves to be exceedingly vigilant and up to Hheir work.
But while saying that I want also to say from information that I have received from various sources, and which I believe to be reliable, that the institution at Portsmouth should be thoroughly cleaned out from one side to the other. It is in need of being cleaned out. There is injustice, petty tyranny, favouritism, and men are being hounded out of their positions through spite. I repeat that the institution should be thoroughly cleaned out and an investigation held ^hat will have the effect of putting a stop to that sort of thing. I live within three miles of the penitentiary and naturally there are a great many of these complaints which come to me. I suppose that a great many of them also reach my hon. friend the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). It is only natural. The parties concerned will apply, I presume, to any member who lives in the vicinity of any of the penitentiaries. The various officials of theso institutions, when they have complaints to make, will hunt up a member and pour their grievances into his ear. In many cases, no doubt, these grievances are only imaginary, but I am convinced that in so far as the Portsmouth penitentiary is concerned the grievances in many respects are not imaginary.
While hon. gentlemen have been expres-singrtheir sympathy for convicts here this' afternoon, I am afraid that the same sympathy is not shown sometimes by the officials for the convicts. I call to mind an incident in connection with the penitentiary at Portsmouth, not during the administration of the present Minister of Justice, I may say, but some years ago. A night guard stopped on his rounds to cut down a convict who was hanging himself in his cell. As you are aware a guard has to go around and wind so many clocks. These clocks are an indication of whether he was awake or asleep during the night. It took some little time to get into the cell and cut down this man wrho was hanging himself. The clock in the morning showed that the guard was a little late in winding it. Being reprimanded for being late in winding his cIock, he explained the reason, stating that one of the convicts was committing suicide, that he thought he should stop him and hot permit him to hang himself. He was told by the official to whom he reported and who reprimanded him for being late: Let him hang, but wind your clock. That is carrying discipline even farther than I believe the Minister of War would carry it. You are talking about sympathy for "convicts, but that particular official

did not have very much sympathy for that particular convict.
Has that remark any reference to our present Minister of War?

Or to any other minister of war, or to any warlike minister. If that statement of mine is true, then any official who showed himself so absolutely heartless as to tell the guards they could let the convict hang who is committing suicide in his cell, and go and wind their clocks, I say that man is not fit _ to hold a position as an official in that institution or in any other institution. I want to say that every hour that passes that such a man is kept in a position of trust in that institution is a reflection upon the department for leaving him in that position. I have stated these facts before; I have asked that the facts be investigated, and I believe it is a proper case to investigate. I want to place myself on record as saying that it will be the more creditable to the Minister of Justice, the sooner he has that investigation and looks into the correctness or otherwise of what I am saying. This is only one instance of wrong-doing which should be looked into. I am merely making these statements to support my contention that there are good reasons why an investigation should be held into that institution.
Some little while ago I was charged in this House with haying advocated the appointment of a man to the position of warden of the Kingston penitentiary because he was an Orangeman, and with being annoyed because the Orangeman did not get the position. I want to say that that is not correct at all. The only man I recommended for the position of warden of Kingston penitentiary was Major Hughes, a gentleman who now occupies the position of inspector of penitentiaries, and Major Hughes is not now and never was a member of the Orange Order. It would not.be anything to his discredit if he were a member of that order; I want that distinctly to go on record as my opinion at all events, whether any person else may think to the contrary. I did advocate the appointment of Major Hughes because he had demonstrated by years of faithful service that he was one of the best men this country ever produced in that line of work. He was spoken of in the highest terms by the late Sir Oliver Mowat, when he was Minister of Justice, by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, when he was Minister of Justice; by the late Sir John Thompson, when he was Minister of Justice, and he was backed up for the position of warden by twenty-five or thirty1 members of this House and a good many influential people outside of this House. I Mr. EDWARDS.
think that is ample justification for_ my advocacy of Major Hughes for the position I thought he was eminently fitted to occupy. However, the Minister of Justice saw fit to appoint him to the position of inspector of penitentiaries, and I maintain that the choice of the Minister of Justice was a wise one. I believe Major Hughes will do good service in that office. A man who has ordinary intelligence-and Major Hughes has more than ordinary intelligence -a man who has ordinary intelligence and has satisfactorily filled a number of positions in an institution like the Kingston penitentiary, must gather a lot of information which ought be of very great value indeed, and I have no doubt Major Hughes will amply justify his appointment by the Minister of Justice to the position he now occupies. It may be that in placing him there the minister has acted more wisely than I would, if it were In my power to appoint him to the wardenship, but the Minister of Justice was quite within his right in appointing Major Hughes as inspector and I am sure no mistake was made, because I believe he will make an efficient officer in every respect.
I wish to impress upon the members of this House my position with regard to tire Kingston penitentiary, and I ask them to bear in mind that the constituency I have the honour to represent comes right up to the borders of the city of Kingston. The county of Erontenac surrounds the city of Kingston; the island municipalities being south of the city and the other portions of my county being north, and east and west of the city. Because of that fact I am necessarily thrown very much among the officials of that institution. I have heard a number of their grievances and complaints; I suppose that where there is any large institution like that there will always be men who think they have grievances, and of course there are many of them who think they tfeve grievances when they really have not. I am perfectly sincere in stating that I do think there is ample justification for a thorough investigation into every department of the Kingston penitentiary, and I am only anxious to have that investigation take place in the best interests of the penitentiary. I believe that is the view entertained by the Minister of Justice. I impress upon him again the importance of having that investigation, and I believe it will mean a lot less trouble to him, a -lot less trouble to all those upon whom responsibility rests for the proper conduct of that institution, if the investigation results in straightening out the tangles and getting everything on a proper working basis again.

I do not want
my opinion to be misconstrued with reference to penitentiary farming. I am not

against farming in connection with a penitentiary, but 1 do think the area of land devoted to that purpose at St. Vincent de Paul is too large. I think one hundred acres would be ample. I agree with my bon. friend (Mr. Edwards) that there is benefit to be derived from education in farming at a penitentiary. As the Minister of Justice is bringing down to-morrow a resolution to increase the salaries of the penitentiary officials, may I be allowed to suggest that he should bring down a penitentiary Bill on the lines which I will suggest. What I will read to the House is a Draft Bill prepared under the late Administration, I think about the month of June last, but on account of the conditions which arose at that time, the Bill was not submitted to the House, although I have no doubt it will be found in the archives of the Department of Justice. This Bill was drafted with the concurrence of my hon. friends from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), Regina (Mr. Martin), and I think all the members *who have penitentiaries in their constituencies. The first amendment proposed by that Bill was the nomination of three inspectors instead of two. I had a conversation with the Minister of Justice this morning, and I think the law will be amended so as to give affect to the suggestion that three inspectors should be appointed, one of whom will be familiar with the French language. Another important change would be made by section 34, which reads:
If any officer dies in the service leaving a widow or any person who in his lifetime was dependent on him, the same gratuity as defined and calculated in previous sections may be paid to such widow, if any, and if not, to any person or persons in the lifetime of such officer dependent on him, or to any person or corporation in trust for any such person or persons so .dependent on him.
We had a case in St. Vincent de Paul where Mr. Champagne died suddenly before he had time to sign his resignation and his family was deprived of the annuity. I think a similar case came from Kingston and one from the West. I would suggest, when a man has not an opportunity to resign before his death, his gratuity should be paid to those dependent upon him. (Reading):
2.	Such gratuity may be increased, by one-half the amount thereof if the death of such officer is occasioned by any injury received by him in the performance of his duty, without fault or negligence on his part, at the hands of any convict, or in preventing an escape or rescue, or in suppressing a revolt, G E. VII., c. 38, s. 34.
3.	No officer on the permanent stafi of a penitentiary, except the warden, deputy warden, matron, deputy matron, Homan Catholic and Protestant chaplain and surgeon, shall be allowed to remain on the stafi
of a penitentiary after he has attained the age of sixty-live.
4.	Every officer, when reaching the age of sixty-live, will ipso facto cease to be an officer of a penitentiary and will be entitled to the gratuity provided for in section 33 of this Act.
5.	Every officer on the permanent force of a penitentiary, who has reached the age of sixty, may, at that time, or at any time between the ages of sixty and sixty-live, tender his resignation to the hon. the Minister of Justice, who may accept said resignation; and, said resignation being duly accepted, the officer whose resignation has been accepted shall be entitled to the gratuities of section 33 of the Act, provided that in each case the conduct of that officer has been good, and that he has been faithful in the discharge of his duties.
I do not need to make any comments. I think my suggestion as an amendment to the Bill is quite clear. I do not think a man of sixty-five years of age can resist a convict who is twenty or twenty-live years old, in the prime of life. How can a man of sixty-live fulfil his duty in chasing a convict and bringing him back?
I thought it my duty to make these suggestions now on account of the resolution which will be presented to-morrow. I shall give notice to the hon. Minister of Justice. If he will allow me, I shall be glad to send him this draft.
My hon. friend from Frontenae (Mr. Edwards) made reference to the appointment of Mr. Hughes. I do not know Mr. Hughes. I am trying to believe that all he said about him is true. There is one thing that the Minister of Justice should explain: what has become of Mr. Dawson, who was a faithful employee of the department for a good many years, a prominent man and an ex-member of this House. He seems to have done his duty while in office. It would be interesting to know where he is now, and fox what reason he left the department. We are entitled to know -whether he has been removed or superannuated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I answered the same
question to another hon. gentleman this morning. Mr. Dawson was transferred to the Department of Public Works, as it was found that his knowledge would be very valuable to that department. There was nothing in the transfer of Mr. Dawson which reflected on him in any way and nothing to prejudice his position or salary.
I am very grateful for the suggestions of the hon. members who have spoken on this subject. There can be no possible question that, in the matter of administration of penitentiaries, there is room for vast improvement. The whole subject of how best to deal with the convict, the man who has so conducted himself as to call down upon him punish-

ment at the hands of society, is a most intricate and difficult, and at the same time a most interesting problem. It is one that has caused a good deal of thought to the officers of the department and, I may say, to myself, since I have occupied the position which I hold to-day, which makes me responsible for the administration of these institutions. I have had in mind some general scheme of improvement in the system. That is something that of course requires to be "very carefully thought out, and a measure to bring that about is one that would necessarily call for serious consideration, and take up in that consideration not a little of the time of the House. For these reasons' I do not propose to attempt to deal with that subject in a general way at this session. I hope, later on, to be able to introduce legislation looking to the improvement of the entire system. When I come to do so, I shall be very pleased to bear in mind the suggestions that different hon. gentlemen have made and I have no doubt they will be found most valuable.
The hon. member for Laval (Mr. Wilson) referred to the existence of a siding at St. Vincent de Paul, which I understood him to say interfered with the advantageous use of the property in the interests of outsiders, particularly with the placing of the derrick at the station there and in the neighbourhood of the station. This matter is entirely new to me. I shall have it looked into. I may say that the penitentiary desires to act as a good neighbour to those who live in its surroundings. If we find there is any inconvenience or disadvantage resulting from the existence of our siding which can be remedied, we shall be glad to find a way to do it.
With regard to the unloading of coal, and this being done at the most undesirable time of the year, that is to say, at the time when it interferes with farm labour, I am told by the inspector that over two years ago instructions were given that arrangements should be made so that the coal should arrive at a season of the year when its unloading would not interfere with the necessary labour upon the farm. If these instructions are not being carried out, it is not because they have not been given. I shall have that matter looked into.
The hon. member referred to the case of a woman who was detained for a day or two at St. Vincent de Paul on her way to the women's penitentiary at Kingston, and suggested that there should be some amendment in the law to prevent the happening of such things. The law expressly provides that, from the time of sentence, the person sentenced to a penitentiary is assumed to be in the hands of the warden of that penitentiary, in the sense that he is the person to whom that, prisoner is to be taken direct. I understand that, as a matter of custom, Mr. DOHERTY.
when it is necessary that a prisoner should stay over for any period of time at any city on his way, the jail is the place where that prisoner is usually detained. The reason for that is simple enough. The prisoner is at the time in the hands of the officer of the court, which is the provincial court; and, in the particular case referred to, I understand the convict was on her way from Quebec, where she had been sentenced, to Kingston, her ultimate destination. The officer who was in charge of her certainly erred in the place which he selected for her to remain in during her stay in Montreal. Moreover, I think the Penitentiary officer erred, when it happened that she was brought there and as a matter of fact did stay there, in not finding some other place in which to confine her. At that time the fact was reported to the department; and, I may say, met with the censure of the department. The officer responsible for it is no longer an officer of the department.

Will the hon. minister tell why the commitment was made to St. Vincent de Paul instead of to Kingston direct? I understand she was confined in St. Vincent de Paul pending the decision of the department as to what to do with her.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand from the inspector that the woman was, on the face of the commitment, committed to St. Vincent de Paul, and the error was in detaining her there. She should have been forwarded to Kingston. I understand that all the convicts sentenced in the province of Quebec are sentenced to St. Vincent de Paul, but in view of the fact that the woman's department is at Kingston penitentiary, she should have been immediately transferred to Kingston.

Is there no woman's
department in St. Vincent de Paul?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

In order to avoid that a woman convict should be sentenced to 'the penitentiary at Kingston even from Quebec, and then she would go direct. The warden at Kingston would have no authority to receive the woman if the commitment was to St. Vincent de Paul.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall look into 'the
matter to see what can be done in that respect. It was a misapprehension that the woman was directly; committed. With regard to the complaint of convicts coing through the village in which the peni. tentiary is to places where their work is to be, done, causing inconvenience to the inhabitants of the village, and also exposing the convicts to be unduly gazed upon, by the public, we should be glad as far a., possible to avoid this. On the other hand,

we endeavour to find work for tliem, and when there is useful work to be done on the penitentiary property, I should not like to undertake absolutely that convicts should not be sent from one place to another. Of course, they should not be allowed, and I do not believe they have been allowed to wander in the village street. But I think the matter can be so arranged that the mere passing of a few convicts on the village street from one point to another would not cause very serious inconvenience. Hov?-
eter, I shall look into the matter.
Reference has been made to the taking of released convicts to the railway station by a guard in uniform. This matter has been brought to my attention', and I have given it some consideration. The inconvenience found is in the guard having to specially dress himself for. the purpose of taking the convict to the station, and then changing his costume when he comes back. But I think we can so arrange it that complaint will not be made. Of course, as pointed out by the hon. member for Laval, it would not do that these men should be let out of the gate of the penitentiary and allowed to stay in the town or village wher<$ the penitentiary is. I believe that the law provides for their being sent out of the town,-I make that statement on the information of the inspector.
The suggestion of the hon. member for Frontenac that convicts might, be used ip working on the roads adjacent to the pem-tentary building is one that I think commends' itself. As the hon. member says, we have done some work of that kind, and 1 shall be glad to look into the possibilities of extending it further. We have also done work of that kind in Manitoba, on the road from Stony Mountain to Winnipeg. It has not only given satisfaction to the people of the neighbourhood, but has proved a useful method of turning to good account the work of the convicts. I have also taken note of the hon. member's suggestion that we might employ these men in making tiles for drains. This whole question of productive work by convicts is one that presents very considerable difficulty. I entirely svmpatliize with the view of the hon. gentleman that it is highly important that we should find some method by which the labour done by the convicts in the institution should inure to their advantage, and more especially should inure to the benefit of those dependent upon them and who by their imprisonment are in fact condemned to a severe punishment, perhaps a more severe punishment than that which falls on the convict himself. I should be glad if we could devise some method by which that most desirable object could be obtained without giving rise to justifiable complaint on the part of free labour outside. For you have to consider that always. Since I first interested myself in penitentiaries, this question has been the subject of thought with me. I have had representations on the subject from people who take an interest in the subject of improving the condition of convicts, and have made inquiries into attempts that have been made elsewhere to meet this difficulty. In the efforts that were made in France, the results, so far as I can find, were not very encouraging. At the same time I am glad to find my view on the principle involved at any rate supported by the hon. member for Frontenac, and I shall be glad to give my best attention to the matter and endeavour to devise some method by which we can gain the desired result. But, as I have said, we must bear in mind that we should not create a condition of affairs that would interfere with men outside engaged in work similar to that to which the convicts might he put.
As to matters of administration complained of, or charges against the penitentiary officers, particularly the matters referred to by the hon. member for Frontenac, I desire to say that it is my purpose to have an investigation into the institution mentioned, and to have it at the earliest possible moment, just as soon as I can secure the services of commissioners who are absolutely qualified both to do impartial justice upon complaints of, or charges against, individuals, and to investigate the methods of administration, and to make such a report thereupon as may be useful to us in our endeavours to improve the system generally. Those endeavours will be materially assisted by the valuable suggestions we have had this afternoon.
Some reference was made to the newly appointed inspector and to some observations that I understand were made upon the recommendation that the gentleman should be appointed to the position of warden of Kingston penitentiary. So far as the qualifications of Major Hughes are concerned, I desire to join most heartily with the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) in what he has said with regard to them. I was so much impressed with the idea that Major Hughes would be most valuable to the penitentiary administration in the highest position connected with it that I appointed him to that position. I think that is the best evidence of my appreciation of his merits and his ability. The hon. member has said that some reference has been made to Major Hughes being an Orangeman and that this was not so. The hon. member said that he would find no fault with him in that regard. I would also say that I would have found no fault with him if he had been an Orangeman, the fact of his being or not being an Orangeman would have made not the slightest difference in my appointing him to a position for which I believed he was eminently competent. Neither in his case nor in the case of

any other man would I be affected by any consideration of that kind. People may differ about matters of this sort, but when you want a competent officer for a particular position, that is no consideration one way or the other in my mind.
Manitoba penitentiaries, $66,700.

In regard to Manitoba
penitentiary, I understand that Colonel Irwin, who has been warden there for a number of years, has been transferred to Kn,0 :ton. Who has oeen appointed warden of Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Captain Ponsford.
What was his previous occupation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say at the mo. ment precisely what occupation he was following at the time his appointment was made. He had previously been engaged in business which involved his controlling and directing very large numbers of men and he had also had experience in the active militia as a captain and was very highly recommended to me. These facts were put before me, I had several interviews with him and I felt convinced that he had qualities which would enable him to perform his duties with satisfaction. Since he has been in charge of the penitentiary I have had the most satisfactory reports from reliable sources as to his competency for the position.
What was his calling in life?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He had been engaged
in the carrying out of very large contracts, principally in connection with building operations, I think.

How many convicts are
there in that penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Last month there were 'one hundred and ninety-five convicts there.

Has a comparison been
made of the actual cost of maintenance per prisoner in the different penitentiaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That information is
given in a special appendix to the report.
British Columbia penitentiary, $90,600.

Some years ago there was a good deal of criticism of this penitentiary and its management owing to the escape of a very noted criminal. Has anything occurred since that shows either a better condition of the conduct of the penitentiary or better arrangements in any way or have the unfortunate occurrences of those years been repeated and if not what is the reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not in a position to say that conditions are materially im-M. DOHERTY.
proved there, but at the present moment the inspector is on his way to British Columbia penitentiary, taking in the others on his way, with a view to make a thorough inspection and examination and report upon the conditions in that penitentiary as well as in others. I do not know that I am in a position to say that we have any special information showing either improvement or deterioration in conditions since the incident to which the hon. gentleman refers.

Have there been many
changes in the staff and in the actual buildings since then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There have been no
changes of importance in the staff, but the large wall which was defective at that time has been completed.
Had the condition of the wall anything to do with the escape of this prisoner?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the convict at the time of his escape was working outside the wall, so that the condition of the wall had no bearing upon the escape, and the respect in which the person responsible was blameworthy was in allowing him to work outside the wall in the conditions that existed.
What is the number of convicts in New Westminster penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: 360 are provided for.
How many convicts are there in Edmonton penitentiary ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There were 197 convicts last month.

From time to time representations have been made to the Government, and to the minister, in regard to the removal of the penitentiary. Can the minister give us any information as to how that matter is now viewed by the Government ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Representations have been made at different times, by different parties, suggesting or recommending the removal of the penitentiary at Edmonton. There have been suggestions that it'should be removed and placed on a different site in, or adjoining, the city, and there have been suggestions that it be removed to some other locality. The last time the matter was discussed was when I had a visit from a gentleman occupying a high position in the municipal government of Edmonton. He was very desirous that we should arrive at some arrangement by which the penitentiary property might pass over to the city, the city providing another site which would still be in the neighbourhood, but not in the heart of the city, as I understand it is at present. As a result of that interview, 1 asked the gentle-

man representing the city of Edmonton to put a definite proposition in writing as to the location of the land they proposed to give us as a site, and to send it to us, and we would consider it. That was a couple of months ago, and we have not yet received any definite proposition on the subject.

Would the minister care to say whether any proposition would be accepted, and if so, what would be the fundamental necessities in such a proposition as to area, the distance from the railway station, and the possibility of having the' benefit of the city utilities, the water works, and so on. If the requirements of the department were known there could be some definiteness in the efforts put forth to meet tnem. But the minister will understand that with properties at high values, and with people more or less keeping an eye on property values, it is not likely that anyone on behalf of the city would go to work and secure a knowledge of a certain area of property that might be acquired, when, after that knowledge had been acquired, the department might say that they did not care to effect any removal, or that the property selected was not suitable for certain reasons. If we could know what the requirements of the department would be in the event of removal, the city of Edmonton would have something more definite to work upon. I know there is a very great anxiety to have the penitentiary removed from where it is, and I am anxious to try to bring the wishes and interests of the _ city of Edmonton to work with the wishes and interests of the Department of Justice. I think both could work together successfully.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The way we look upon the matter is that the penitentiary is satisfactorily situated as it is. As I understand, the citizens of Edmonton are desirous that we should remove it. We are not exactly in the position to define conditions upon which we should go out, because we are not in the position of wanting to sell. The city comes to us; we are satisfied with the present position. We find many advantages in the present site, which they say they desire to acquire. Under these conditions, it-seemed to us fair to ask the city, wliat is your proposition; you are the people who desire the change. I think we would be disposed to give every consideration to a proposition in the interests of the city of Edmonton, consistent with our duty as administrators of the penitentiary, but it seemed to us that the initiative lay with the people who desired the change to be made, rather than_ with us. If the change involved no detriment to the public service, and was carried out in a manner that would be just to the penitentiary, we would be disposed to give it every consideration. However, I will consider the matter from the point of view of the hon. member.
Has the minister any objection to stating who the official was from the city of Edmonton?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At the moment I cannot recall the gentleman's name. He was an alderman of the city. I do not mean to say that he was speaking officially in that capacity, but like the rest of the citizens he was interested in this matter, and he came to see me, and we talked the matter over. As I have said, I made the suggestion that he should endeavour to see if -some definite proposition could be made. He was not in a position to speak of any particular site. If he had been in that position, and if we had had a proposition to exchange sites, we would have been in a position to look into it, and to deal with it. But it is 'difficult for us to go looking around foT sites. We might select what we considered a good one, and find that it was not possible to secure it. The city on the other hand knows what sites could be procured.

The alderman who
visited the minister would probably be Alderman Smith. I understand he was given authority to interview the department regarding the. Temoval of this penitentiary, and that the city government had made arrangements to purchase land, within three or four miles of the city, which would be suitable for penitentiary purposes. They had also arranged, I understand, to extend the street railway system on the understanding that the Government would surrender their property in the city of Edmonton. As the hon. minister is aware, the property, as at present situated, comprises 100 acres in the very heart of the city. It is not only that the location is objectionable, but this vacant land in the heart of the city is detrimental to the best interests of the city, and I think it would be in the interests of the Government that these conditions should not prevail much longer. If the city is prepared to give the Government a suitable situation and possibly erect a building, such as they have on the present area, I presume the Government would have no great objection to the change being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not prepared to say offhand that merely on this basis we would be prepared to act. We have to bear in mind that we have an exceedingly valuable property, an asset of this Dominion, and when it comes to a question of exchanging, we would have to look to the question of what we are parting with and the value of what we are receiving. I

do not mean by that to say that no consideration should be given at all to the position and interests of the city of Edmonton and that we should act absolutely with the view of wanting to treat this as a purely commercial question, but I say, and I am sure the hon. gentleman will agree with me, that the comparative values of the property to be parted with and that to be given to us is a matter that we have, to consider. Then the peculiar advantages that our present site has for our special purposes will have to be taken into consideration as compared with the advantages that would attach to any area which may be offered to us. It is difficult for us to make a definite answer to a general proposition. It is a, matter that does not seem to me that we can come to any conclusion upon unless the department is put in possession of precise information as to what the city offers to us in exchange for what we have. I have the best disposition towards the city and to consider what is in the interest of the city of Edmonton as well as what is in the interest of the Dominion as a whole.

There is a certain area
surounding the present penitentiary. The whole of that area is not practically available for the purposes of the penitentiary as the railway tracks run across a part of it. I do not know how much of the property is occupied, but it would probably he twenty or thirty acres. It might be presumed that that is a small area for a large penitentiary. If the department would consider that a larger area less conveniently situated would answer the purposes of the department as well, or better than a small area -conveniently placed, as this is, there would be some ground for the city of Edmonton to go on and try to make an arrangement. But I am afraid, from what the minister has said, that we have not made much through the change of Government, because the argument he puts forward is about the same as that which his predecessor put forward. It was up to the city to show cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is difficult to accept or reject a proposition that is not made. That is our proposition pure and simple.
I said to the gentleman who came to me, and I say it again, that I would be prepared to deal fairly with any proposition that is made to me, bearing in mind the importance of this matter to the city of Edmonton, as well as trying to do my duty as representing the Dominion. But I cannot say offhand that, if a site is offered to me, I will accept it. No doubt the advantages of a larger site would be a matter to be considered. I can only say that I am quite open to any other suggestion that may be made and I am prepared to consider it as Mr. DOHERTY.
fairly as I am capable of doing. I can realize how important it is to the city of Edmonton and I shall be glad to meet their views consistently with doing my duty on behalf of the Dominion.
Mr. OLIVER. I do not wish to press the minister unduly and I do not wish to suggest that he is not acting in good faith and consistently with his position, but it is my business to place before him and the committee the position and views of the people whom I represent. It is conceded generally, as was stated by my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Wilson) and my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), that it is in the public interest as well as in the interest of the penitentiary itself, that the institution should not be inside the city. It should not be inconveniently situated, hut it is better that it should not be surrounded by population. In Edmonton the situation of the present penitentiary iST absolutely surrounded by population. While it is not in the centre of the city, it is measurably centrally located. I have not very full knowledge, but it is probably more within the city than any other penitentiary in Canada. That being the case, the citizens of Edmonton are inclined to the view that it is not in the interest of the city, or in the interest of the good administration of the penitentiary, or of the country, to have the penitentiary located there,^ and that it should be located outside the city. The area that is now occupied by the penitentiary is admittedly small compared with the ordinary requirements of a penitentiary. Therefore, to take the further step, they believe that the penitentiary should have larger grounds, which it can only have by being outside the city. There are certain advantages possessed by the penitentiary and the department by reason of its location, in that it has .street cars, city utilities, electric light, waterworks, and all the other conveniences. These are great advantages and they possibly could not be supplied at any serious distance outside of the city. If the Government would say that the use of these utilities was an essential condition to the location of the penitentiary outside of the city, the people dealing with the matter would know that, with respect to any location that they desired to secure, "they must not go out of the range of city utilities. If the Government would insist on the use of the utilities, convenience to the street cars, convenient access to the steam railways, and a certain distance from the city, the people could go and do business. If these utilities were not insisted upon, of course, it would make the task very much easier and a still larger area of land might be secured at more reasonable

figures. It is not- with a desire at all of tying the Government or the department up to making an exchange that I am presenting this matter to the minister, but I would like to get what would be the minimum that the Government would accept in the way of the use of utilities, distance from the centre of the city, &c. If we could get the minimum the Government would accept in these three particulars, we could go on and see what arrangements we might make; not tying up the Government to accept what we would think, but we would have something definite to go on in making these preliminary arrangements. On the other hand, if it is not possible to secure a change of location, there is no reason I can see from the standpoint of the Government or of the city, for retaining as penitentiary property that part north of the railway track. It seems to me that part might be disposed of because it is not of serious value to the penitentiary for penitentiary purposes. The fact is that the lines of the Canadian Northern railway and of the Grand Trunk Pacific cut this part off for penitentiary purposes from the rest of the ground, and it might very well be disposed of.
The other point is that the wall around the penitentiary is only a board fence, and I would almost make the criticism that the reason the convicts remain in the penitentiary is because they like the board and the situation of the place. There does not seem to be any reason why they should stay there unless that be the case. If it is intended to maintain the penitentiary in that place, a more sufficient and permanent enclosure should be erected so that the officers of the penitentiary be not at the risk of their lives as they are to-day, with that continual inducement to the convict to escape. There have been several escapes. There have been several escapes or partial escapes from the Edmonton penitentiary, and_ probably the minister does not know that the then assistant warden was done to death in the penitentiary some years ago. The conditions are that" if the penitentiary is to remain where it is there should be improvements which would tend to the retention of the prisoners and the safety of the officers. I am satisfied there might be blame attached to the officers for escapes, which I think would be entirely unjust, under present conditions. It is because it is necessary to make extensive permanent improvements in the present location that I would urge in the interests of the administration of justice that ultimately, although perhaps not at present, it is desirable the locality should be changed and the conditions approximately more closely to those universally accepted as conditions which should surround a penitentiary.
Saskatchewan penitentiary, 553,800.
How many convicts in the Saskatchewan penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A daily average of one hundred. It is situated at Prince Albert.

Is it within the city
limits?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: About three miles from the city.
What area of land surrounds it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
About six hundred
acres in the penitentiary reserve.	-

That bears out very
strongly the argument I addressed to the minister in respect to the Edmonton penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
An increased area
would probably be of advantage at Edmonton, and having listened to what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) has said, I shall be glad to think the whole matter over and see if there is some practical method of meeting his views.

If the minister would let
me have an idea whether he would insist on access to city utilities, or whether he would be willing to accept a situation not in touch with such utilities, it would greatly help.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will think it over.
Has the penitentiary at Prince Albert electric light, sewers, and water supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The penitentiary has its own sewers and water supply, and the electric light is supplied by the city.
Expenses under the Pecuniary Claims Convention with the United States, $2,500.
What claims are these?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a commission
sitting to determine a number of pecuniary claims which the United States Government, the Government of Great Britain and the Government of this country had agreed upon to submit to the determination of that commission. There is a great variety of claims, most of them of very long standing. This commission, which began its sittings a week or two ago at Washington, is to pass upon these claims, after the particular claims that are to he submitted have been determined by the respective parties. Will the minister explain how this money is to be expended?
It is for camp and drill ,. instruction, care of arms, postage and for trumpeters and signallers' degrees on qualifying for a certificate.

Has the minister decided upon any policy regarding the care of arms? Some small armouries have been established in different parts of the country. If an armoury of any size is built and arms are placed in it, it seems to be the custom that they shall be taken care of by the caretaker of the armoury, whoever he may be. Here is a case in point. I think that probably the first instance where a small armoury was built in connection with a public building, that is, a combination of an ordinary public building and an armoury, was in the town of Hartland in my^ constituency. I think one corps of militia is now housed in the armoury. I ' understand that somebody was appointed to build the fires, to keep the place clean and to act as general janitor of this public building.
When?

Some time within the
last six or eight months. The building was completed only a few months ago. I have found that the captain of the local company has been notified that henceforth he has nothing to do with the arms of his company, they are taken out of his charge and placed in the charge of the janitor of the building. It may seem a very small thing to the minister, but it may be a very important matter to the men interested. In the first place, he says the responsibility is entirely upon him to look after those materials, keep them clean and keep them in order, and if there is any remuneration he should have it. But, more than that, when inspection day comes around, if there are deficiencies, the captain is responsible, and the amount will be taken from his pay, and he will have no way of recouping himself. Has this matter been brought to the attention of the Minister, and will he under the circumstances, leave the matter to the competent officer connected with the company who understands these matters-and has given good service?

I have no knowledge of the case referred to. The question of the care of these armouries in public buildings is a matter of rather serious import, and so far as I am concerned, I have refused in many instances in which it was brought to mv notice to have the public building used' for company purposes. They entail, as the hon. gentleman says, the appoint-

ment of a caretaker, and the furnishing of fuel, and, so far as I am concerned, our policy-which we are gradually getting into shape-is to turn these buildings over to the Public Works Department and erect small halls of oar own. Furthermore, we have not yet quite developed our policy in relation to the caretakers, but I find that many of these gentlemen have done little, if anything, except to cater to the companies in the evening occasionally when they are in their quarters. Accordingly, we are rearranging the whole scheme of caretakers, and we purpose seeing that they attend to business where they are r.ecessary and that they are retired where they are unnecessary. My own idea is that the officer in command of the company in a small place should be the man to take charge of the armoury. Of course, where the dual policy is in vogue-it has been in vogue for some time, and I have not interfered with it except in cases of necessity- where the caretaker of the public building looks after the room and arms, the officer in command of the company still gets half the pay. But we have the whole matter, under consideration. Some 'of my officers have personally inspected a number of the armouries and in scarcely one solitary instance have we found them satisfactory. Toronto was satisfactory; Hamilton was more than satisfactory; Ottawa was simply scandalous, and there were other places where the men were not earning their money or doing their duty. A system will be devised to meet the case.

I am glad to hear the statement made by the minister. With respect to the armouries which are wholly military and entirely under the hon. minister's department, I do not think there is any complaint. We have a very competent caretaker who was removed for special purposes, and another gentleman apnointed in his place, of whose qualifications I make no complaint. He is a good Tory, and that was enough to secure his appointment.

He can do his work, I
will guarantee.

I wish to say, to the credit of the minister, that he stood by the militia and against the caretaker. The caretaker would not allow the band in the room because they made a noise, the minister interfered and allowed the band to go in-and make all the noise they wanted to. However, that is not what I wished to speak about. So far as the Woodstock drill hall is concerned, no fault has been found, because a man was appointed who received sufficient pay to justify his giving attention to the matter; and, so long as I had anything to say about it, I had a very competent man who certainly looked after
everything in good shape. But, when you come to the small dual armoury and Public Works building you have a different state of affairs. You have a civilian appointed as caretaker. I do not speak with reference ' to the-gentleman in the case to which I specially referred, because while this is in my own constituency, I do not even know his name. But in such cases, you have a civilian appointed who knows nothing about militia matters, and the captain of the company feels that a great injustice would be done to him if he were compelled to hand over these arms to a man who is not responsible, and yet the captain of the company himself is held responsible.

Is the hon. gentleman
certain we have a man there? I have a fairly good memory, and so have my officers; and we have no recollection of appointing a man in any way under the Militia Department. The man must be a public works man.

I do not know. I have a file of correspondence here- which, though in a sense confidential, yet which I shall be glad to show the minister if he so desires. Although, it might be-what do the minister's men call it?-derogatory to these in command to have an officer write to somebody else
This is a free country.

This officer wrote to me.
I am not finding more fault than is necessary, but as I understand, it was proposed that the care of these arms should be taken away from a military man and placed in the hands of a man who was appointed by the Public Works Department. The captain objected, and I think with great reason. Whether the matter has been carried out or not, I do not know. I hope the minister will tell me that it will not be carried out.

I have no recollection
of such a case. I have no knowledge of any place in Canada where we have an officer in a public works building.

But the minister has
knowledge of cases where the Public Works Department building officer has been given charge of arms and equipment.
No, not at all.

This item covers provision for the storage of arms and accoutrements. That was the cause of a good deal of difficulty when I was a member of the Government, representing a constituency and supporting the Government. I hope that there will be less trouble now that the responsibility is on other shoulders. But it is not in regard to drill halls I wish to ask, but in regard to the provision for a country

squadron. What is the system in the department' in regard to caring for the accoutrements of, say, a country squadron of mounted men?

The system is the same as my predecessor pursued in relation to individual squadron headquarters. It would be impossible, even in a large number of years, to make provision for each squadron or company headquarters, but we are adopting a policy of inexpensive drill halls for squadron headquarters where we can store these supplies and we make the cost about equivalent to the rent of buildings we would have to obtain for storage purposes. These headquarters buildings also serve as places for the men to meet and drill.
In looking over the correspondence, I find that the caretaker was a former militia man, but he is not now and has not been for some years.
I shall look it up.

As there is not a dollar
spent in my constituency for militia purposes, I am perhaps qualified to ask what is the total amount asked for this year for militia purposes and what is the increase over last year and the year previous?

Have you the year before?

No, I have not those
figures with me.
Where is the chief increase?

The increase is chiefly
an increase in the number of militia.

Would the minister add
to the figures here given the amount that is being spent by the Public Works Department for militia purposes?
I have not that information here.

I thought
the minister was going to transfer the construction of buildings used for military purposes, such as drill halls, from the Public Works Department to the Militia Department and construct them under the supervision of his own engineers.

When the minister says an increase in the number of militia, does he mean an increase in the number of men and horses and the cost of equipping these men and horses with guns, armaments, &c.? Would the minister give the number of men and horses for the two years?

Yes. For 1911-12: men, 41,015; horses, 8.880; for 1912-13: men, 48,140;
horses, 9,758 were trained in camp. That is about 1,000 more horses than were trained the year before and nearly 5,000 more men. This year the total increase over last year will be 9,151 men and 3,528 horses, which is a pretty large increase.
