House in Committee on Bill No. 207, respecting a Patent of the Commercial Acetylene Company of New Jersey.-Mr. Maclean (Souin York). (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

In the absence of the promoter, this Bill stood over on the last occasion it was up. It is a Bill that affects patent rights, and it certainly should not go through without some responsible statement being made as to how far private rights are affected by it.

I would suggest to the Government the necessity of bringing in some sort of legislation next session to get rid of all this nonsense of placing people in the position they previously occupied, and which they lost on account of negligence, because in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred these Patent Bills are for the purpose of relieving people of the results of their negligence. It used' to be the case that the patentee had to show some reason why he should be reinstated, but now we seem to have reached the point where a man can come here and say that he was negligent and had not paid his fees, and he is then reinstated. If it is right to reinstate a patentee in that way, it is not fair to make him pay two hundred dollars, besides solicitor's fees. It is taking up the time of Parliament. There should be some way of reinstating patentees without taking up the time of Parliament, I have made this statement before, and I offer it as a suggestion to the Government, li they are going to continue the present course of renewing every patent right that has expired by reason of negligence, the patentee should be relieved of the expense of coming here.	.	[DOT]

I entirely agree with the remarks of my hon. friend, especially when a patent holder has been negligent in his duty and when he places his Bill and explanation in the hands of some member who is also negligent in his duty, thus wasting the time of Parliament, I en-
Mr. OLIVER.
. MAY 27, 1913
tirely agree with the hon. member that the time of Parliament should not be wasted in this way by men who do not appear to have any interest in their own business.

A system nas grown up that is almost vicious in its results. We are getting more and more lax every year. Men come here now and claim reinstatement as a matter of right. They pay two hundred dollars and get their patents renewed. Up till two or three years ago we made the applicant show some reason why he should be reinstated. I can tell my hon. friend that three years ago a matter came before me professionally which meant a lot to the parties I represented. They were willing to establish an industry in my town, and expected to employ forty or fifty men if I could get their patent renewed. But I could not see any reason why it should be renewed, for they had simply been negligent. I did not want them to come and perjure themselves, and I advised them that I did not see any way of getting their patent renewed, and the patent was not renewed. Now, if that case came up to-day, all I would have to say to them would be, pay two hundred dollars and the fees of the solicitor. It is a great change, and I have doubts whether it is a change for the better. Parliament gives a man protection for a certain number of years by reason of his invention. It is a premium to the man for his diligence in inventing some article or piece of machinery. That is all right. But Parliament gives him that protection on certain conditions, one of which is that at the expiration of six years, if he does not pay his fees for renewal, his rights are gone. It seems to me that the public have some rights in this matter as well as the patentee. The man who has not enough interest to pay his fees, does not deserve to be reinstated, and I do not see why Parliament should come to his rescue, simply by asking him to pay $200.

The patentee, who
comes from Toronto, was here last week and was exceedingly anxious that this Bill should go through. He appeared before the committee, and the Bill seemed to be all right.

The Bill is to grant an extension of time for one year for the manufacture of the patented invention. The hodlder of the patent is a Belgian, and did not know the manufacturing requirements of the Patent Act. An English company has taken up the invention and proposes to establish a factory in Canada within a year if the patent is reinstated. The facts were brought out fully before the committee, the Deputy Minister of Agriculture being present, and the committee was satisfied that a case had

been made out. That is all the explanation I have to offer. It is similar to other Bills that have been before the House. It is very similar to the case covered by the Bill that has just gone through, and I would ask the committee to give it the same consideration.

What is the patent for?
_ Mr. MACLEAN: I cannot explain that in detail. It has been before the committee and the minister, and it has gone through the Senate.

The Bill states that it is:
A patent, issued under tlie seal of the patent office of Canada, number sixty-seven thousand six hundred and seventy-nine, dated the eighth day of J une, one thousand nine hundred, for certain new and useful improvements in the method of storing acetylene, and that the said patent has expired by reason of the non-payment of the fees required by the Patent Act.

I understood from the
promoter of the Bill that this was an extension of time to allow for the manufacturer to begin.
Yes.
But I understand now from the Minister of Customs reading the Bill that it is a case in -which the patent right had expired four or five years ago, and it is to renew it.

The purpose of this Bill is to grant an extension of one year to allow of the manufacturer of the patented invention, and with that extension they will immediately undertake the manufacture of the patent ik Canada.
Is this for making acetylene?
J ust for storing it.
I am sure the hon. member will give the committee suitable information as to what the process is.

It seems to me that the
principle of extending these patents is altogether wrong. The patentees have a reasonable time in which to comply with the law, and if they do not take enough interest then we should not extend the patents by legislation in this House. If they do not comply with the law the patents should become public property.

In any event such legislation should be introduced by the Minister of Agriculture, and he should take the responsibility of recommending the passage of these patents in the House; it should not be left to a private member.

I am
quite willing to allow the Bill to stand until the Minister of Agriculture is here if anybody wants that, but inasmuch as similar Bills have gone through the House, until such time as the Government establishes a fixed policy, exception should not be made of one particular Bill.
I agree with that.

I object to this continuous renewal of patents. If the people who take out patents do not take enough interest to get them renewed, we should not renew them here. I would like this to go as a warning to those whose patents have expired that they will not be renewed in this House.
Hear, hear.

It is a remarkable position to place the House in, because here we are renewing a patent and no one in the House knows what the patent is for. I do not wish to oppose the Bill, but the House certainly should have some information about it. Inasmuch as it relates to acetylene, we ought to have more light on it.

House in Committee on Bill No. 208, respecting a patent of Maurice Delvigne.-[DOT] Mr. Barker. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
As this also relates to a patent, and as the hon. member in whose name the bill stands is present, it would be in order to have an explanation.

This Bill is on behalf of a Belgian, who invented an explosive, and who employed people here to get a patent for it. In ignorance of our laws-I do not put that forward as a genuine excuse for the Rill-he did not realize the necessity of renewing it, and allowed the time to expire. When he found out the true situation he at once tendered the money. The patent was granted only three years ago, and the bill protects anybody who may have begun to manufacture the explosive in the interval, so that there can be no harm done. The patentee is paying everything that he would have paid if he had known what was expected of him. The Bill passed the Senate, and they thought it was a proper Bill. It also passed our committee, and, subject to what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) says as to these cases being dealt with in this way,_ I cannot imagine a better case for reinstatement than this. This Belgian had no knowledge of the fact that he was risking anything; he thought he had his patent Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
secured, and he offered to pay the money, whenever he found it was necessary^ In the Bill there is an express clause providing that any person who has begun to manufacture the explosive is protected, and that he may continue to manufacture.

Did I understand my
hon. friend to say that the patent was granted only three years ago?
Had the party to manufacture according to the provisions of section 38 of the Act?
I think that was so. He did not begin within the three years, but he was ignorant of the necessity for doing so.

This Bill will of course go through, but it only illustrates the point I was making. If there is a principle of patent law known to every man who has had anything to- do with patents, and to every solicitor in Canada who ever took out a patent for a patentee, it is that the patentee must commence to manufacture the article within two years, or come within the provisions of section 44 of the Act. I do not want to say anything 'offensive about my hon. friend's Belgian, friend, but no man can be so innocent, who would wish to get a patent in Canada and who would employ a solicitor foT that purpose, that he would not know that he must commence to manufacture the article within two years-. It is not possible, yet the man comes here and says: I did not know. That only illustrates the truth of what I said a little while ago that men ought not to be placed in that position. If it is right to renew these patents and allow them to evade the law, let us do it in a less public way than this; let us hand it over to the' Department of Agriculture, to the Patent Commissioner, to .some board, or to some public body, that can take these matters up, deal with them solely on the merits of each case and reinstate a man in his rights, if it is proper that he should be reinstated, but do not bring him to Parliament and make him state to the world that which it must bother him to state, or get somebody to state it for him.

I quite agree with,' what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) says that it may perhaps be well to have some remedy other' than that of coming to Parliament. But that is not the law yet. This man is a foreigner, a Belgian, he had people acting for him here and he had no notion that he was risking everything. The moment he found out the position of affairs he acted very promptly in coming here. The original patent was issued in 1910. If you can have any excuse under the present law I

think this is a reasonable excuse * in this case.

I do not want to oppose the passage of this Bill, because, as my hon. friend says, this case is as good ais a number of other cases that have received the assent of Parliament. But clearly the principle is vicious. My opinion is, however, that it is not a change in legislation 'that, is wanted but that it is a change in administration. These are private Bills, it is true, and it has not been the custom of the Government to take control of private legislation. That is probably a sound principle under most conditions, but where private legislation is continually and repeatedly sought, as it has been at this session, to set aside the law which embodied the mind of Parliament, i think the time has come for the Government to take the matter in hand and either to propose to Parliament such changes in the law as would be right and fair or else assume responsibility for private legislation of this character. I am putting this before the Government with all respect and without any desire to find fault, but I think that the conditions which have been 'shown during this session with regard to the renewal of patents are such as reasonably call for definite action and for a definite policy by the Government in the administration of the patent law.
1 Mr. ROGERS: I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), and were it not for the fact that the session is about drawing to a close, I would have no hesitation in saying that we would introduce legislation to cover the points which he has suggested. In the meanwhile I would venture to suggest that it would be well for the holders of patents to consult with their legal representatives, and if their legal representatives continue to be negligent irr the future, as they have apparently been in the past, I have no hesitation in saying that the Government will next session introduce legislation to remedy this condition of affairs.

When this item was
under consideration at six o'clock, I was anxious to get from the hon. minister an understanding of the conditions that are now imposed or observed by the department in dealing with the care of arms and accoutrements of country squadrons. I assume that it is the desire of the department to establish mounted corps throughout the western country; that is. as the agricultural population become well settled and fairly prosperous, it is hoped that the young men will find recreation and interest in connection with the militia; and that, as a matter of fact, the young men growing up in the prairie provinces will be the great strength of the militia force, especially so far as mounted men are concerned. Therefore it is important that the department, in its arrangements, should take cognizance of the conditions prevailing in strictly rural settlements. One of the difficulties is the care of arms and accoutrements in a purely rural community or where the community is almost purely rural. What is the policy of the department in providing for the care of arms and accoutrements of a squadron of militia in a rural community?

The policy is to give $100 allowance for each squadron for care of arms. The officer or someone in connection with each squadron looks after this himself. He usually provides his own building, sometimes an upstairs room in his own dwelling or a hall. The policy is, wherever there is a goodly sized town or even a country village with a squadron, to build a small drill hall. The custom has been to put an armoury in the public buildings. I have figured up the additional cost to the Public Works Department of these armouries in public buildings. I find that a very convenient little building can be put up as a drill hall in each of these towns for less money than it takes to place an armoury in a public building, the reason being that armouries in public buildings are more highly finished than the ones that we put up. It will take a good many years before we can catch up, because there are about eight or nine hundred of these units throughout the

country. Therefore we must rent for a long time. Where we do not rent, we give an allowance of $100 which recompenses a good man. For example, Wetaskiwin is a large town. The officer there did not want to be bothered with the matter so we rented a building. The rent is a little more than the allowance. We use the building for drilling the men in the evenings, and in that way get an additional advantage out of it.
The experience I had was that the allowance was under most circumstances entirely inadequate for the rent of a building that would take proper care of the arms and accoutrements of a mounted corps.	.
For saddlery, it is.

The necessity of having a water-tight and a good and roomy building for taking proper care of the saddlery is not recognized in the amount of money available" under that arrangement. I wish to emphasize, as strongly as I can to the minister the' absolute necessity of having either a larger allowance or a more elastic arrangement than formerly prevailed, especially in regard to mounted corps. While $100 might be quite sufficient to make provision for the arms and accoutrements of an infantry company, it would not be at all adequate for saddlery. There is another feature of it that I am sure must have struck my hon. friend. The saddlery that is required for the militia force might very well be used in civil life if it is not properly cared for, whereas the arms and accoutrements of infantry are not liable to be used except when the men are on duty. Unless the saddlery is kept under proper control, it is liable to become missing or the worse of weaT.
While the minimum rental allowance that the minister speaks of may be adequate to provide a place to store the arms and accoutrements of an infantry company, it absolutely is not adequate, nor anything like adequate, to provide suitable storage room for the material of a mounted squadron. I take it for granted that it is to the prairie country that my hon. friend looks for the development of his mounted forces. That is where the mounted service is most likely to attract the favourable consideration of the young men. But if they are met, at the very beginning of their organization, by expense or inconvenience, it is distinctly a discouragement, for they are very apt not to take the interest in it that we all wish them to take. I urge the hon. minister to make a larger minimum for the mounted companies, recognizing the greater value and greater bulk of their material, and that he provide greater elasticity in the provision according to the circumstances. Because, Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
while in a very small country village it may be possible to get rental at a low rate, when you take a thriving and a growing town, this accommodation must be paid for. It costs money, and if not paid for it cannot be had. I had great difficulty in impressing that on the late Minister of Militia; I hope I shall be more successful with the present minister.

We are working along the very lines the hon. member has laid down. In most cases, wherever an application is made and officers report upon it, we have increased the allowance to $125, $150 and so on. I may say that the value of the clothing and equipment of a cavalry regiment is $36,000, and it pays from an economic point of view to look after it.
Do I understand that the captain of an infantry company receives the same for looking after the arms o)E the company as the officer commanding a troop of cavalry?
No, the infantry get less.
That is what I thought, but the hon. member for Edmonton seemed to think that the minister assumed that they got the same amount.
The infantry get $80 and the artillery and cavalry more. We increase them because of the greater value and bulk of their material and the greater need of taking care of them.
I suppose the Minister of Militia will do as he has a mind to-we may take that for granted.
No, he is amenable to reason.
Certainly.

The hon. gentleman
says he is going to establish small drill halls all over the country-nine hundred or a thousand of them.
No, my hon. successors will do that; I will not be here that long.

I believe I had the
honour of having in my constituency the first armoury and public building in Canada. Does the hon. minister think that he will get better results from the small buildings he -is going to build than from the combination? If he is going to nave a building big enough for a drill ball, he is going to spend many thousands of dollars. He cannot get architects and draughtsmen to design and put up cheap Duildings for him. It cannot be done with public officials.
They could do it, but they will not.

No, it cannot be
done with Government officials. They will

design expensive buildings, and the minister will have to build them. If he is going to put up a buiiamg of any size he will run into five figures at least and when he has the building, he must have the expense of caretakers, fuel and so on. But in the combination building, one set of officials, one caretaker, one expense for fuel and light will do the whole thing. The smaller building may satisfy the vanity of my hon. friend, but it will not conduce to economy for the ratepayers of Canada.

I do not want to wTangle across the floor of the House, but my engineers have looked into the matter. As yet we are very economical; I do not know what we may be in ten or twelve years. In every instance where we have been asked to join in having one of these combination buildings and armouries-which, I am sorry to say, is never used for drilling purposes, but is used for smoking, cardplaying, spending the evening and not for the upbuilding of the militia-when we have inquired into the cost of the thing and the architects of the Public Works Department have given us figures, we have found that -with the extra money needed to produce the combination building, we can produce a commodious drill hall suitable for anv company in Canada to drill in, we are doing it as a matter of fact. If the hon. gentleman will come down to the department, the engineers will show him the plans-if necessary, will show him the buildings.
What do these buildings cost?
They cost $6,000, $7,000 and $8,000-and the building for a battalion $16,000. This building has rifle galleries in it and everything.

Are they wooden
buildings?
No, brick buildings.
What -size?

In the larger towns in

kinily explain the enormous increase in this item as compared with two years ago? There must be some good reason. I have gone over the matter hurriedly, but I understand that there is some $600,000 or $700,000 of an increase.

Air. HLlGHES: 44,000. Last year we had 48,140, not including the city corps. Then we had 9,758 horses, an increase of 5,000 Mr. OLIVER.
men and nearly a thousand horses. It is an increase of about 60 per cent. That may be a very slight increase. But, I find at page 38 of this report that the vote provided $1,169,000 of which $155,000 was unexpended and that left practically $1,000,000. There were no city corps drilled in camp the year before last. Does my hon. friend
mean to say that the city corps did not drill in 1911-12?

Well, they got a lot of money if they did not.

It seems to me that if we do not put the brake on this militia expenditure in some way or other there is no telling what the end is going to be. It is nothin? short of a scandal that we are going to spend between $10,000,000 and $11,000,000 this year on militia in a peace-loving country as Canada is, in which there is no more danger of a possible invasion than there is of an earthquake overtaking the whole Dominion and wiping it off the face of the earth.
There was one the other night.

I do not know hardly
what to say. I have no doubt that I will be taken to task in certain quarters for presuming to criticize the militia estimates. It may be said that I am not loyal and all that sort of thing, but I am willing to take all the responsibility of what I am saying now. When it comes to spending $11,000,000 on our militia and when we come to think of the way in which the militia has been increased by the present minister we should st-on and think what it all meansi. It is something terrific. When the hon. gentleman took charge of the department two years aeo there was an expenditure of about $7,000,000.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon:	He will find it in this report if there is any question about it. I find here that the total expenditure for 1911-12 was $7,579,000. A portion of it was unexpended, so that it brings us practically to $7^000,000. Now the minister has got it in two years, or practically one year because he took the estimates of the old Government for last year, up to $10,500,000, making an increase of $3,000,000 for one year, and he is going to add half a million to that in the supplementaries. There is between $3,000,000 and $4,000,000 of a jump in one year. What does he want? Is he going to give us a standing army of 100,000 men? Do we want that? Does he think the people need it? I never heard anyone who had any idea that we would be called upon to use the militia against an enemy except the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) who the other night said that in case of war between the United States and Japan it may be necessary to police the borders of the Dominion to prevent our people from sending a few thousand bushels of wheat over to the United States and selling it at the best price they could get for it. If this money was going to, the men who spend their time and devote their energies to the militia service, I would not feel so badly about it, but out of an expenditure of between $10,000,000 and $11,000,000 we have less than $2,000,000 going to the men. My hon friend in his orgies of extravagance has only about $1,830,000 for the men. What on earth becomes of the rest? It would make an interesting story if my hon. friend would take half an hour and try to explain it. Here we have eight and a half millions of money being squandered-I will not say squandered, but being distributed to everybody else, but the men who ought to have it. Surely $1,800,000 ought to be enough for the whole thing. If you take the report and look at page 35 it will give you some little idea of what they do with the money. I find that in the year 1911-12 they spent $243,000 for eighteen-pounder limber wagons
and $366,000 was paid to the War Office on account of thirteen and eighteen pounder guns.
Then, there is a very interesting item of $20,000 for inspection of small arms and scabbards. There must be a lot of men drawing big salaries for doing nothing when you can squander $20,000 for inspecting
13,000	rifles and 20,000 scabbards. The Minister of Railways yesterday told us he was going to take up the rails on a few miles of railway down in New Brunswick, because the road did not pay running expenses; he was taking away from the people a railway connection they had had for forty years because it would cost a portion of $13,000 a year to maintain it, but here we are throwing away $10,000,000 on the militia and $20,000 for the inspection of a few rifles. That may satisfy the ambition of the Minister of Militia, but it is getting to be a very serious matter in Canada. I know that the minister and many of his friends will find fault with me, and I presume his fiiends will say I am the one disloyal man in Canada, but I mean every word I am saving and I hope the public sentiment of Canada will be aroused to such a pitch that they will put a stop to this nonsense. If they have $10,000,000 to spend on militia, an excess of three and one-half million dollars over last year, they could use that money in a hundred different ways to really benefit the people of Canada. There is a great demand for the development of our natural resources and f<ft facilities for carrying on our commerce, but it would seem that the whole occupation of the Minister of Militia is to build up a great army and a great war party in Canada for what earthly reason I do not know except it be the glorification of the Minister of Militia.

No one is charging the
hon. member with being disloyal; at least, I am not; he is merely getting off his annual speech on the militia question. He was always tame when his own party was in power; he used to take a fling once in a while at these fuss and feather fellows and then he would subside. I am delighted to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) again on this question. I want to tell him that I am not spending this money; it is the people of Canada who are demanding this. I want to tell him that we are only drilling-

Ten or fifteen per cent
more than ten years ago when it cost only two and a half million dollars.

I am not responsible for ten years ago. I am dealing with the present. We are drilling this year about 56,000 men and 13,000 horses. Let me tell my hon. friend that the people of Canada to the extent of about 70,000 more are de-

manding the right to train themselves and be trained to defend their country. It is the people who are demanding this, it is not the Minister of Militia. They are demanding the right to train themselves to defend their homes and their firesides and their country, and I tell the hon. gentleman that so long as I am Minister of Militia I am going to do my level best to give them a chance to do so, and I am going to do it as economically as it possibly can be done. It is the right of every citizen in the Dominion to train himself, and be trained to defend his country and if he demands that right, I am not the man to tell him he is not to do it. So long as the system is voluntary the people must pay for it; if the system is compulsory, then it will make it much more economic, but whether it is compulsory or whether it is voluntary, arms must be furnished and guns must be bought. My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) is an old artillery man, and he knows the cost of a battery of artillery; it costs money, but it is money well spent in the upbuilding of the country. You may look around any part of the universe you choose and show me a race that is not possessed of the military spirit, and I will show you a craven and degenerate race. Show me a part of the world where the people neglect the defence of their homes and their firesides, and run after graft in docks and dredging and railways and I will show you a degenerate race.
Mr.^GRAHAM:	You will have to take
that back when you get into the Railway Department.

I am not going to the
Railway Department. It is presided over by a gentleman of great ability and good looks and splendid capability.

It is said
that he is coming out and you are going in.
'' Mr. HUGHES: Not at all. We have nearly
60.000	voluntary militia now and we have
35.000	cadets trained this year in Canada for the modest sum of $10,000,000.
The modest sum.

My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) speaks of only $2,000,000 reaching the men. Has he ever figured it up? I can give him the expenditures in his own county in recent years and it rolls up to a considerable amount. I am glad to see my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marci]) take an interest in militia matters now. He is generally complaining that his county does not get anything and I am sorry to say that not much money has been spent on militia matters in his county, although there has been a lot of hard-earned money of the people of Canada blown in along the shores of the gulf Mr. HUGHES (Victoria, Ont.)
of St. Lawrence, and the maritime provinces, and Ontario and the West, and I 'do not know that it has built up the manhood of the nation any more than is proper, but I do know that the money spent for the training of the militia makes a better set of men in the Dominion of Canada than we would have if the money were not so spent. I make no apology for my aspiration to have 100,000 men trained and I make no apology direct or indirect for acceding to the demands of the people. As far as I can induce my hard hearted colleagues to go, in the expenditure of public money for* militia matters, I am not going to make an apology.
They are a parsimonious lot.

Yes, they are. When
70,000	people rise up in their might and demand the right to be trained, and I have to tell them we have no money to do it, it is pretty hard, but I am glad to say that a great many of them have organized and are training themselves this year without any money.
Are the women interested in this?

I am glad my hon.
friend asked the question. When I took office I found the good women of the Dominion of Canada down on the militia system of this country, and rightly so to a large extent; I found that they were refusing to allow their sons to go into the camps, but I want to tell my hon. friend that the good women of this country to-day are right behind the militia movement and urging it on in every way they can.
Has the minister closed the canteens?

There never have been any canteens since I have been Minister of 'Militia to be closed. I wish my hon. 'friend (Mr. Carvell) to be good enough to blame the people of Canada but not to blame the Minister of Militia. I point out 'to him that at Confederation it was understood that one-tenth of the annual revenue 'of Canada was to go for the development of the militia of this country and I point but further that I am far from the estimate of one-tenth of the revenue of the Dominion of Canada in my expenditure. That was the understanding with the Imperial Government at the time of Confederation, and I am two or three million dollars yet within that estimate.
M>. OLIVER:	You are catching up
'fast.
' Mr. HUGHES: I intend to catch up fast and I intend to help the people of Canada who are demanding the right to train

themselves to defend their homes and their firesides. I am not urging them to do it. They are coming forward in thousands demanding the right. I have yet to see why they should not be accorded the right. I am sure my hon. friend would rather pay the trifling sum that is required for the training of these extra men than squander it in useless dredging and in erecting wharfs where boats will never tie up.

My hon. friend mentioned the words ' compulsory system ' a moment ago. When one-sixth of the estimates were being considered, somebody asked him what his views were. I think I am entitled to have his views on that question. He has expressed his views outside of the House during recess, and I think we have a right to know what his views are.
The hon. gentleman has no right to ask me what my private views are, directly or indirectly.
Your views as a minister?

My hon. friend has no
right whatever, and I have not accorded him the right to ask what my private views are or my views as a minister. When the matter is decided upon by the Cabinet I shall be glad to let him know what their views are. He has stated that I have made certain statements in the papers. I would like to know what the statements are.

It is reported in the
newspapers.

That is a different matter. I stated that in South Africa Louis Botha requires each man who does not turn out and perform his annual drill to contribute the sum of $5 a year to the treasury of the South African colony, in order to maintain the defence of that colony and of the Empire, to keep the old flag flying, as he says, in any part of the world. A similar idea is carried out in Australia, in Switzerland, and in other parts of the world. That is the system adopted in countries where there is practically universal training. I have not said what my views are on the question.

, My hon. friend says that he is compelled to spend all this money. While I believe we ought to have a small militia force in Canada, I see no reason why it should be any larger than it is to-day, if as large. The militia force has not increased to any great extent in the last ten years. The number of men trained is not very much greater. I admit there is an enormous increase in the number of horses, and probably some of these may be necessary, because, if you create a mounted corps you must of course provide it with horses. Horses are expensive, but a number of horses that have
been paid for are absolutely useless. That is what I am grumbling at. There is a company in my own constituency called the No. 1 Company of Engineers, which used to be called the Brighton Engineers. Annually they take to camp twenty to twenty-five horses. They have nothing for these horses to do, and I have seen them standing up at the picket line for the whole ten days. These horses have to be fed and paid for. Last year I pointed out to the hon. minister that he was making a big mistake in taking all these corps to Petawawa. He was determined, however, that the Minister of Militia should be glorified, if ever a man was glorified.

Against my own wishes, 1 carried out the policy that my hon. friend himself inaugurated by supporting his own Minister of Militia, because every plan that was carried out at Petawawa last year was formed by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia. I point-blank refused to carry it out this year.

My hon. friend may blame his predecessor in office if he wants to; but he cannot blame me, because I pointed out to him the difficulty of transporting horses a thousand miles when it was not necessary.
I am not blaming anybody.

I told my hon. friend be would have trouble if he transported these horses a thousand miles, and he has had trouble and nothing but trouble. I asked for a return some time ago and I got an order for it showing all the correspondence regarding claims for horses in the Kent field battery. I find here that about twenty per cent of the horses taken to Petawawa got sick. The department had to pay pretty large claims. The men were dissatisfied, and I am sorry to say that in some cases their claims have not been paid. I have here the claim of one of the drivers who had two horses, one of which was very sick and wa3 laid up for three or four weeks. This driver can get no satisfaction whatever for the loss of his horse, although he has made claim after claim. All this is due to the unbusinesslike policy of my hon. friend in taking these horses a thousand miles when there was no necessity for it. It is such things that cause this enormous expense, without any returns from it. This year I am glad to see that he is taking all these corps to Sussex which is only a short distance. That is all right. The people of Canada are not demanding this expenditure half as much as the Minister of Militia is. I know something of the trouble that the officers are having in regard to recruiting. I do not believe there is a corps in Canada that is not violating the regulations in

order -to fill the companies. Men under age and over age are being taken on. That shows the difficulty the officers are having in getting their corps filled up. When my hon. friend tries to tell us that the sentiment of the country is so great that he has got 70,000 men demanding the right to be trained, I say that this is what he has got. He has got about seventy officers who are demanding the right to form corps and to get these men to train, for their own glorification. It is not the men who want it; it is the fellows who want to be officers, and who want to create these corps. They go around and coax the young men and the old men to come into the corps. Then my hon. friend comes down to Parliament and says. See what we have done. If my hon. friend would ask the ordinary people, he would find that they do not want this militia expenditure. I know, in the atmosphere in which he is living, he hears nothing else, and he does not want to hear anything else, because it is music to his ears when these fellows come to him from all parts of the country and say to mm. We want a corps here and a corps there.

Liberal members and
Tory members.

I know who they are-just the class of men I have been describing. However, I have pointed out one of his blunders, and one way in which money is being squandered. Not very much-[DOT] only $10,000 or $15,000.
Ten times that.
That just shows how easy it is to squander $100,000. I am not opposed to a reasonable militia force. I believe, probably it is necessary; I am opposed to this unwarranted squandering of public money.

What does the hon.
gentleman think the militia force is necessary for?

To put down labour
riots?

Not labour riots particularly, but any disturbance in which the civil power requires the support of the militia force. The militia has been used for that, and may be used for it again. But we have now a permanent force that will attend to that and we do not have to Mr. CARVELL.
call out the militia for it. If there is anything to be added to this answer to my hon. friend, I do not know what it is. At the time of the South African war, we sent some men to South Africa. But we did not send only the Canadian militia; the militia formed the nucleus and supplied the machinery by which men volunteered.
We sent no organized corps.

No. But though I
have seen but one occasion for the use of militia in my lifetime, I would not say to disband the militia. I say that every country ought to have a reasonable militia. But I object to this enormous increase of expenditure. When we get to $7,000,000, that ought to be the time to quit, but the Minister of Militia thinks it the time to begin, and if he is allowed to have his way, instead of' $10,000,000, he will spend $20,000,000. He proposes to spend ten per cent of the total revenue, and as the revenue is expected to be $200,000,000 next year, that will mean $20,000,000.

I did not think it was
so high. Fine!

That is the estimate of the Finance Minister, and I take him as an authority. The Minister of Militia will find opportunity to spend it-if it was $40,000,000, he would spend it, and much of it, no doubt, on just such useless affairs as in his transportation of horses to Peta-wawa. He will not repeat that expenditure, because he has had his lesson, but he will do something else next year that will be just as bad. He has to do it to spend the money. He will buy-
Automobiles.

Yes, no doubt he will
buy more automobiles. But I do not wish to discuss the automobiles now; an item will come up on which that discussion will be more in order. But I think the Minister of Militia should tell this committee that he is going to quit this enormous expenditure of public money.
"Mr. PROULX: There is some criticism in the press of the army of high officials that are drawing high salaries, yet without work to do. A Government paper speaks of $200,000 spent on 'Scotch and soda officers', meaning, I suppose, officers who spend their time at the club &nd have no work to do.

Let me say a word in reply to the hon. member for Carleton. In 1911, while a Government supported by my hon. friend was in power, the camp was
assembled at Petawawa, exactly the same as last year.

The hon. gentleman
knows that we took the men, not the horses.
In 1911, men and horses went to Petawawa. In 1912 my predecessor had laid out the plans to go to Petawawa, and to take the officers and men. I came into office-

Does the hon. minister mean to tell me that the Woodstock field
battery took their horses to Petawawa?
They did or-
They did not.
I tell him, the Tenth did.
The Tenth may have done so, but they did not. Nor did they in 1911.
They change about. Some New Brunswick batteries took their horses last year, and some did not.

I do not want the
hon. minister to state to me things that are not true.
I am not stating things that are not true. What I said was that the 10th brigade and the 11th brigade- six batteries-
That is not New Brunswick,
There was the Moncton battery, and that is in New Brunswick, as the hon. member should know.

That does not mean the
3rd brigade.

They came from New Brunswick. They did not bring their horses, but horses were hired for them here. But others did bring horses. The Woodstock battery did bring horses last year; I presume they did not the year before. But that camp was laid out and carried out, as I stated, last session on lines not approved by me. If the hon. member will look at 'Hansard' be will see that I pointed out that this camp was going to be carried out against my judgment, but because the plans had been laid down by the officers of the Department and by my predecessor, I would carry out their plans for that year, but it would not occur again; and it has not occurred again.

I think the people of Canada are in favor of maintaining an adequate militia force. Also I hold that we are not expending enough money on our militia. I see by the estimates that we are spending for the drill of militia only $1,730,000. The active militia of Canada are underpaid.
I agree with that.

Take the militia men obliged to bring horses to camp for $1 a day, when they can get $2 a day for every one of their horses. Remember, too, the class of men we bring to camp, and paid only half of what they could earn by staying at home. The people of Canada seem to have the opinion that an annual camp is a picnic. Let any gentleman come to camp, and he will see the sheer hard work these men have to undertake. From five o'clock in the morning until six o'clock at night they are working hard. What I object to- and I am speaking now only of the active militia-is: First, the men are underpaid; second, that the horses they supply are underpaid; third, that too small a number of men are drilled; and, fourth, they are not drilled for a sufficently long time. Take, for example, the tactical programme, look at the programme they have marked out for us. I want to object strongly to the new tactical work that has been marked out for the militia of Canada to go through unless preliminary instruction is provided for the regiment before going to camp. Without that it is absolutely impossible to take these men into camp and ask them to perform the work set out in this scheme. We have only twelve days' drill. There is one day to go in, one day to go out, one day for Sunday; that is three days; there are nine days left. Then, we have squad drill, one day. Squad drill, as you know, is the groundwork. In the regular army, a recruit is required to be instructed in squad drill for at least three months. The next day is for company drill. Then they have a day in battalion drill. In a city corps they will be working night after night for weeks and months before they are able to properly perform battalion drill. Then there is one day for brigade drill. Then allow for wet days and "what have we left? Two more days. Then there comes the field day, the tactical day. The tactical day is supposed to be a miniature fight. The red body is sent away down some place, and the blue some place else, and then they march a great number of miles and are supposed to come together-and, according to the rules, the battle has to end at twelve o'clock because they have to have dinner. What I want to impress on the members is that in the first place there is not enough money spent on the active militia, in the actual training, and there is not sufficient time spent on the annual training. Any man who has had any experience in the active militia knows that, with the material that we have in Canada, our men can learn more in one week than men in other places can learn in a month or even a greater time. If our militia service had instructors there would be a great improvement in the

conditions. That is the great want of our militia. The present minister and his predecessor are not responsible for this. Who are responsible? I do not know, but I know, as the commander of a regiment for a number of years, and as the commander of a brigade for a number of years, that it is " impossible to _ get a sufficient number of efficient instructors during a camp. Therefore I say that the first _ thing we want is a large increase in the number of instructors. Our men are keen to .learn, our officers are keen to learn, but we have not the instructors. We want a corps of instructors whose services will be available throughout the year. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) is an old militia officer, I have seen him in camp for a great number of years; he has been a most efficient officer, he knows the requirements of the militia as well as I do. The present Minister of Militia is an old militia officer. I believe that the present minister's heart and soul are in the militia. I believe that he will do his utmost to increase the efficiency of the militia; but we do want a radical change in some respects. We know that before the Hon. Sir Frederick Borden, the late Minister of Militia, became minister, the militia of Canada was sadly neglected. Under his efficient control and management the militia of Canada advanced at a marvellous rate-
Hear, hear.
-as regards efficiency, esprit de corps and everything that makes up a militia force.

I understand the hon. member for Carleton (Mr-. Carvell) to take a view of the military affairs of Canada which is incompatible with the proper consideration of that subject, at any rate in my opinion. As I understand him, he is in favour of a permanent force. He thinks that anything in the way of civil war or labour riots, industrial conflicts, whatever it may be, might be put down by a permanent corps. He believes that it may be supposed to be able to put down such troubles as those if they arise. For my part, I am altogether against that. I do not believe in that son of thing at all. A permanent force, so far as I can understand military affairs, which perhaps is not very far-but in this I think I am voicing to a certain extent the views of some of the people of Canada-a permanent force is not needed in Canada; what is needed is some such body as the militia which affords a system of training for the young men, not necessarily to fore each other, and go at each other or to attack people inside or outside of Canada; its greatest Mr. McLEAN (Sunbu-ry and Queens).
usefulness is as a system of discipline. I understand that the Minister of Militia has some such view in regard to militia affairs and that that is why he is developing so rapidly the cadet, system; it is to introduce a spirit of 'discipline and esprit de corps into the youth of Canada. I would therefore take away the two and one-half or three million dollars provided for the permanent corps in the estimates, which would reduce the estimates by so much, and add one-half of that amount to the development of the militia corps. _ That would have the effect of perhaps bringing down the estimates to a certain extent and of developing the young man of Canada in the way that it seems to me they ought to be developed. I cannot express myself too strongly against the theory that we should provide a permanent force in Canada for the suppression of our own people.
What is the hon. gentleman going to do? We promised to Great Britain to man the fortresses a few years ago, and how is he going to do that if he takes away the permanent corps?

I would reconstruct
that agreement, if necessary.

I was there once, and
why on earth the Militia Department bought the place, or should send men there every year, is something I cannot understand. It is nothing but a great sand plain, and would kill any horse and almost any man who goes there.

My hon. friend
is the only man who has visited Petawawa camp who speaks of it in that way.

ugly place in my life.

Perhaps my hon. friend'
knows all about it.
