speechtext:
I want to tell my hon.
friends opposite that the present Minister of Militia is carrying on his department in a businesslike manner.
If that solder is an illustration, I doubt it.

Some years ago I was
an officer in the militia, and I can tell my hon. friend how these things are done. The Government make a contract, or at least they used to do so, with one firm, or with one man to supply the articles required for the camp. The man usually ran a store in the New Brunswick camps, and I think I can tell my hon. friend who will run that store this year at Sussex.
The same man?

No, I do not think so. The job was always put up to tender, but my hon. friend will see to it this year that some good Conservative runs the store. The man who ran the store furnished all the articles required for the camp. That is the reason that the man is able to sell these different varieties of articles and that is exactly what is done at Pembroke or Petawawa. The only question -is whether the articles were supplied at a reasonable price or not. I do not know and I do not care very much. I am willing to admit that the Militia Department was run just about as extravagantly when my friends were in power as it is now. About the same class of officials were running it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the policy is different.
The policy is different? The only difference is that they have transformed it into a straight Tory policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not at all. As far as
Petawawa is concerned, no Tory need apply when the late Administration was in power.

I expected to have some explanation from the minister with regard to the remarks made by mv hon. friend from Queens and Sunbury (Mr. McLean). He is an active member of the militia, one of those who was in command of the Canadians who went to England at the time of the coronation, and he states that the annual camp is a farce, and that the money spent is squandered. Does not my hon. friend think that the time has come for a sweeping reform? I admit that my hon. friend is a good officer, and we have to expect some reforms from him. He has been told by a fellow-officer that the organization is a farce from beginning to end, and yet he sits there silent and does not have any explanation to offer to the committee. I would like to know before we. vote $10,000,000 if any reforms are going to take place and if he is going to see that our young men are properly drilled by the necessary number of instructors. There are no instructors at these camps or, if there are, they are perfectly useless, according to the statement made by my hon. friend from Sunbury and Queens. What is the minister going to do about it?

I am delighted to see
that my hon. friend from Rouville is so energetic and so greatly interested in the welfare of the militia. The hon. member for Sunbury and Queens never said there was no organization of the militia, and therefore I do not need to answer what my hon. friend did not say. My hon. friend spoke of the instructors, and we will come to the matter of instructors in good time. We have trained upwards of 8,000 instructors in this country, and I purpose initiating a policy of training a great many more officers, but I do not want to enunciate that policy until I am ready to cany it out.
Where are they?
From the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I want them by provinces.

I do not have to give
them by provinces because I have not got them. I could give the cadet instructors by provinces but I do not propose to do so until the item comes up. i do not propose to trespass upon another item. The pay of the men has been doubled in the last ten years, and the pay for horses has been increased 25 per cent this year.
What is it now?

$1.25 a day for all
classes and $1.50 for heavy gun horses.
Mr. CARVEiLL.
The men are being very well looked after as well as the horses, and I agree with the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens that until there is compulsory training, which seems a long way off, you cannot expect men to turn out and give their time and money to tha upkeep of the militia force without getting some fair recompense tor it. I admit that the men are not getting as much pay as they are worth, but they are being paid as jvell as most militiamen the world aver.

This is a most important item of the estimates, it is a large item and it brings up a very important question. We have had in this House during the last three or four months a lengthy discussion with regard to Empire defence. We were instructed by our friends that Canada was not able to undertake her proper part in Empire defence because she did not have the men and she did not have the spirit to take that part; that is to say, the defence of the Empire by sea. Therefore, we were required to vote a sum of money to he expended in providing battleships which should be manned by British sailors under the direction and control of the British Admirality. The discussion we have had to-night would almost indicate that, so far as the land forces are concerned, we are far from perfection and, by the same process of reasoning that we have' heard during the past four or five months, instead of further carrying on this militia force at an expense of $10,000,000 because that force must be for the defence of the Empire-it is not for the defence of Canada, because Canada has not needed defence for a matter of thirty years-we should hand that money over to the British War Office. I want to ask the minister if, on that process of reasoning to which the House was subjected during so many months it would not be the part of wisdom, of patriotism and particularly of loyalty to the Empire, if, instead of carrying on this system of drill which my hon. friend from Sunbury and Queens says is not efficient, instead of maintaining the camp at Petawawa, which my hon. friend here says is not useful for the purpose, instead of bringing out men to drill, as I understand some hon. gentleman to say they only go from time to time and not as a regular matter of enlistment, it would not be in line with the policy that the Government, of which the minister is a member, and his leader and his party, have insisted upon so strongly for the past five months, having regard to all these facts, to take the $10,000,000 and hand it over to the British War Office for expenditure by that office in defence of the Empire.
And bring back General Hutton.
Carried.
No, I would like to have the answer of my hon. friend.
I did not catch the question. Will the hon. gentleman repeat the question?
I am asking the minister, in view of the policy which he has supported in regard to the defence of the Empire, in view of the facts that have been brought out in the debate, does he not think that-

What are the facts to
which the hon. gentleman has referred?

As he has heard. Is he
not required, in carrying out principles to which he and his- Government are pledged, to change the tenor of this vote and hand this $10,000,000 over to the British War Office for the defence of the Empire?

If the hon. gentleman
would be good enough to point out the facts to which he refers, I would be delighted to answer his question, but I cannot assume the question on his premises until I know what they are.
__ Mr. OLIVER: If the Minister of Militia is not able to give this Dominion a more efficient and effective military service, is 'it not for him to say to the British War Office: Here is $10,000,000; you know how 'to spend it better than I do; spend it for the defence of the Empire.
_ Mr. HUGHES:	I have heard.no criticism against the militia to-night, from any gentleman who is in a position to know anything about the militia. My hon. friend from Queens and Sunbury (Mr. McLean) has upheld the militia, and has pointed out that we should spend more money, to which iny hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) objected. The hon. member from Queens-Sunbury says further that we should provide for a longer annual training tout to that I object because the men of this country cannot leave their business for more than the present number of days to devote to annual training. I stand here to say that Canada has a militia to-day which is second to no militia in the world. I have seen the Swiss militia and they cannot compare with the Canadian militia; I have 'seen the French regiments and I can pick out fifty per cent of the militia regiments of Canada which are just as good as the best of the French regiments; our militia regiments are just as good as the best of 'the German regiments and as good as the British regiments except about twenty per 'cent of them.
Did my hon. friend see 'the German regiments?

Yes.
' Mr. LEMIEUX: Last year?
' Mr. HUGHES:	I was not there last
year, I was there the year before, and I 'may say that I was almost induced from half a dozen high sources to go to Germany last year but I had no time as I was attending the British and French manoeuvres.
; Mr. LEMIEUX: What about your Vancouver speech?
The Canadian militia to-day stands second to -no militia in the wide, wide world.
Did the minister state in this House that the Canadian militia are efficient ?
I did, a large percentage of them.
Am I to understand they are serving willingly and at pay which does not compensate them for their lost time ?
Yes.
They are enthusiastic and capable ?
Yes.
I do not wish to misunderstand what the minister said; did the Minister of Militia say they were enthusiastic and capable ?
Fire ahead, I did.
They are enthusiastic, capable, efficient, and there are 45,000 of them ?
More than that; 73,000.
We have 73,000 men in Canada whom the Minister of Militia says are efficient ?
Nearly all of them.

And are enthusiastic and are willing to make sacrifices for . their country, and are willing to do military service at loss and cost to themselves, and yet the Minister of Militia is a member of a Government and a member of a party which during five months in this House has placed a libel upon the people of Canada; has persisted in it; has insulted the manhood of Canada by the declaration that Canadians would not do by sea what they do by land. I say that Canada resents that insult; the people of Canada fling that insult in the face of the Prime Minister and his Government and his party.

We are anxious on this side of the House to assist the minister in getting through his estimates, but let it be understood that he must civilly answer a fair question.. We have demon-



strated during the last six months that ye can stay here and continue to ask him questions if necessary. Now let us start out with a fair understanding. The minister says he has trained 8,000 instructors last year.

I said 8,000 cadet and
militia instructors were trained in Canada up to the end of last year.

Well, that would mean ever since Canada was civilized and we had a militia, but many of them are hors de combat now. One of the great difficulties in the militia of Canada is the lack of efficient instructors. Does the minister mean they have trained 8,000 men in the last year, or how many have they trained ? What number of instructors are there at present ? And what provision are they making for instructing each individual company or regiment.

The number of instructors we passed last year, including cadet instructors, was: Nova Scotia, 593; New Brunswick, 620; Prince Edward Island, 194; British Columbia, 272; Ontario, 193; Alberta, 389; Manitoba, 346; Saskatchewan, 117; Quebec, 189.
We are not talking about cadets just now. How many thoroughly competent instructors has the minister to send around the different military camps and corps this year ?

We have already about one hundred and twenty competent instructors for the militia regiments, and there are others attached to the regiments themselves. The permanent corps is being instructed so that a large number of men will become competent instructors in a few years. In former times men of the permanent force were not called upon to be instructors at all, and were never given the opportunity of drilling a squad. Instructions have been given out for some time that each man shall have the opportunity regularly of standing in front of a squad and drilling them. In a short time we hope to find out who have the quality of being instructors and who have not. We are pursuing that policy in the hope of developing the whole force as far as possible, so that within a year they will be pretty well qualified to be instructors. These instructors are sent from corps to corps during the winter and to the camps in the summer. In answer to my hon. friend from Queens and Sunbury (Mr. McLean), I may say that in place of having the permanent corps of Canada to act as fatigue men and markers in the butts, these men are to be attached to the various Mr. CARVELL.
forces as models and, those capable, as instructors.

As a member of the active militia, and as having been present at camp for a number of years, I wish to complain of the want of instructors. The Minister of Militia states that a full corps of instructors will be provided in the future. I agree with the hon. minister in that policy. In the past a large amount of money was spent on the permanent corps, and the men of that corps were not trained as instructors. It would require at least one instructor per company, although there should be more.
Another objection is this. It always seemed to me that we should have in Canada a permanent corps of instructors, composed of officers and non-commissioned officers. A non-commissioned officer^ in order to be an efficient instructor, requires ability and training. He ought to be paid a salary in accordance with the work he performs. We want more officer-instructors. The Minister of Militia will agree with me that the officers of a corps are occupying a very doubtful position when a sergeant comes out and drills the corps. I think you should have officer-instructors, at least one per regiment, one per battery of artillery, and so on with the different branches of the service.

We have practically
developed already a system of training officers, and you may include in that instructors. At the present time, in order to take a commission, one must pass the junior, intermediate and senior examinations for the British army. The papers have to be examined in Great Britain. The consequence is that very few officers have the opportunity of qualifying. The militia officers cannot write on these examinations as they are shut out. We have therefore developed a system, after a good deal of study, of examinations in and for the Canadian Militia, so that any private, sergeant or officer may have the opportunity of writing, when he feels qualified to pass the examination. At the present time there is no such opportunity for a Canadian volunteer. In this way we hope to have a large number of young men, especially in connection with our university corps and the various cadet corps throughout the country, thoroughly qualified in all that pertains to the instruction of any_ corps that we might wish to deal with in our annual camp. There is no intention that a young man, who passes an examination entitling him to command a regiment, shall command one. It merely gives him his certificate of knowledge. He might stand in the ranks, as other men have done with similar

certificates, as a private or a subordinate officer and work his way up gradually. We would have, however, at the disposal of the country in time of need a large body of men thoroughly qualified as instructors. In the course of a year or two, I hope there will be young men in every village, town and city of the Dominion who will take no second place to any instructor, whether he be of the permanent service in the Dominion of Canada or elsewhere.
Is there any discrimination in the policy of the Department as between city officers and country officers?

No, I know the case my hon. friend refers to. I looked into the matter. My hon. friend refers to the case of an officer appointed for command over another officer. These promotions come from the commanding officer in the various localities. Unless for very special reasons and unless our attention is drawn to the matter, we accept the recommendation of the district or brigade officer. We take it for granted that they do their duty. If an officer is specially reported against as not being able to manage his men, and the other man reported over him, we do not know the conditions and the thing goes through. I know the case the hon. gentleman refers to, though I did not know it until he first drew my attention to it. Otherwise, I would have made inquiries. The officer was promoted over another, because that other was not considered competent to command the squadron.

The officer in question is
too good a soldier to have the matter brought up in Parliament and ventilated. A great injustice was done to that officer, and it is not a matter of yesterday, but has apparently been going on for years with other officers. It has been a great discouragement to officers in that regiment. I dp not know to what extent that kind of thing prevails through Canada. While I am on my feet, and in order that my hon. friend from Carleton may not be alone in the statement that we are going on too fast with militia expenditure, I desire to add a word. To-morrow morning, when the people read the statement of the minister that the policy of his department is to spend ten per cent of the Dominion revenue on militia-
The minister has not said it. What the minister said was that that was the policy laid down at Confederation by agreement with the Imperial authorities.

And the minister is approaching it very rapidly. Take the position as we have it, and not holding the minister down to>
that statement. The expenditure now has reached ten or eleven millions of dollars. It will possibly run up, within ten years, to an average of $15,000,000. Is that extreme? I think not. Now, the Department of Agriculture has done a good deal of advertising, and has sounded trumpets before it to announce that it is going to spend $10,000,000 in ten years for agriculture. Their expenditure will be quite insignificant compared with that of the Militia, which will be $150,000,000 in ten years. I think that the members on both sides, and the members of the Cabinet, should say to the Minister of Militia right now that this must be stopped, that it is not the policy of the people of Canada to spend $150,000,000 on militia in ten years.

The hon. gentleman does not seem to be posted. He forgets that agriculture does not belong to the Dominion, per se; it belongs to the provinces, and is so treated by the provinces. In the states of the American union the militia is under control of the state, and the building of drill halls is under the same control. The matter is very largely under the control of the officers of the militia. Suppose that, let us say, in Rochester, New York, a drill hall is required, the officer in charge simply notifies the municipality that it must furnish a drill hall of a certain size and build, the people have to pay for it. And the militia are paid out of the state vote, just as in the Swiss cantons to a very large extent. Therefore, these items do not appear in federal expenses in those countries. But in Canada, the cost of militia building, the upkeep^ of the militia come out of the Dominion treasury. The vote for agriculture does not.

Mr. Chairman, I have not very well understood the remarks made a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. McLean), but I do not think I am mistaken in saying that he has approved of .the expenditure asked for in behalf of the Canadian militia, and even then he does not find it sufficient. Whatever the hon. member may think about it, I believe that if in the last election he had used the same language when addressing his electors, he would not occupy t'he seat he now occupies in this House, and that if he undertakes to repeat those words at the next election, his electors shall think otherwise than he does and shall make him aware of it.
As to the hon. member for Carleton, I share his views. The military expenditure is not at all in proportion with the amount we spend for agriculture. Having read the list of the main estimates which amount, for the Militia Department, to $10,479,065, and of the supplementary estimates brought

down the other day and which run up to $438,240, I find the total expenditure to be $10,917,305. To my mind, this item is extravagant and should not be voted by this House before a substantial deduction has been made.
When I was a candidate at the election of 1908 and of 1911, I reproached my opponent with not having protested against the military estimates being run up to six or seven million dollars. Instead of six millions we have to face, to-day, an expenditure of nearly eleven million dollars for military purposes only. This is something extraordinary and I think the hon. Minister oE Militia himself would be surprised to witness how unwelcome is the increase which he asks us to vote, if he took the trouble of consulting the hon. members, even those sitting on this side of the House.
The financial conditions of the country, prosperous though they be, do not allow us to dispense with the rules of prudence. Moreover, we are not in South America or in Europe, where the nations are always exposed to war. We have but one neighbour, and we cannot be sheltered against his attacks by means of an expenditure which is extravagant, if not useless. I think the hon. minister of Militia should reconsider his figures before asking us to follow him in the direction of an extraordinary increase as regards the military estimates.
I know also that the people of our country are opposed to such policy which will have no other result than to bring us considerable harm even from our friends.
I -wish to enter my protest against any military estimate which we may dispense with. We have no rebellion to fear. We are far from the time when we might dread the blows of those fools and rascals of 1837 and 1838-to use the words attributed to the hon. 'minister-whose attention I would call to the fact that there were such fools and rascals in Lower and Upper Canada as well, of different race and tongue, but fighting for the same principle of a responsible government, for a government of the people by its mandatories. .
Those fools and those rascals were men of spirit and men of honour, whose doings have gone down to posterity, and the memory of those martyrs of liberty is deep-rooted yet in the hearts of their offspring, a few of whom are in this House and do not like the memory of those heroes to be tainted with impunity. We do not want military men in our country as much as we want farmers. There are always too many people who try to live at the worker's expense.
Let us encourage the farmer and the manufacturer; we shall never spend too much for this purpose. If foodstuffs are scarce and dear to-day in our country it is Mr. BOULAY.
because the consumers exceed the producers in number, and we should help the latter before all.
Those are the few remarks I had to make on this subject and, really, I cannot approve of the extraordinary expenditure which is asked for in the estimates and *which means an increase of nearly three million dollars as compared with that of last year.

My imperfect knowledge of the beautiful French language has prevented me from .following in detail the remarks of the hon. gentleman. I shall see his words to-morrow in 'Hansard', and, I * hope, will have an opportunity to answer him.

In regard to this item for drill expenses, if my hon. friend is going to insist on keeping control of the militia and military expenditure instead of handing it over to the Imperial authorities for better management in their hands, of course he will have to listen to such advice as is offered to him from time to time. I do not speak as a military man, but as a citizen interested in the well being and well doing of the militia force of Canada. There have been placed before the House to-night by those in close touch with military matters statements that would indicate that conditions are not all that would be desirable. There are difficulties of recruiting for the camps. There are difficulties amongst the officers of regiments here and there. Let me suggest that the militia organization depends to some extent upon social conditions, and as social conditions have changed in this country that system which was adequate, sufficient and satisfactory twenty or thirty years ago is not so to-day when conditions all over the country are considered.
I speak first of the case of officers. Officers are required to undertake large expense which they undertake for their own pleasure and for the good of the country as prominent, patriotic citizens. Amongst these expenditures they must provide their uniforms. I do not know what would be considered proper to happen to a man who would .suggest that that which has always been in military matters should cease to be; some terrible thing might happen; but I am going to risk it, and I would say that in my humble judgment when an ordinary citizen of Canada, with a good share of patriotism and so circumstanced that he is able to give attention, time and energy to the work of being an officer of a company or battalion of volunteers, when he gives the proper time and attention to his own training and to looking after the force of which he is an officer, he has done all that can be reasonably required of him by the country.
Hear, hear.

To ask him to pay for
expensive uniforms is simply an imposition and takes the matter out of the realm of patriotism and efficiency and transfers it into the realm of financial ability or social aspiration. That I do not think is good for the force and it is not' in accord -with the present condition or spirit of the country. I am quite aware that as matters were in Canada thirty, forty or fifty years ago that was a perfectly right and proper idea, probably the best idea on which the system could be based, but I desire to press upon the attention of the minister that the condi. tion of Canada has changed so that that system of dealing with the officers of the militia is not suitable, does not bring the best results, and, so far as western Canada is concerned, is to a great extent impracticable. I know we have volunteer forces in the West and probably they will size up very well with those in other parts of Canada, but if so it is because of even greater sacrifices made under more difficult circumstances by the men who are taking the responsibility of acting as officers in those forces. I do not know what would happen to the minister if he should suggest such a thing as that the country should buy and pay for the uniforms of the officers. He has a reputation of doing as he likes, and I only hope he will like to do what I suggest. I have no personal feeling in the matter as I have never been a military officer.
You would make a gallant colonel.

And I have very little
hope of ever being one; but I would like to see matters run on a basis of fair play, and I would like to see a maximum of efficiency and a minimum of expense. I have no doubt there would be a very serious outcry against such a departure, not from the taxpayers, although there might be some objection from them; but I have no doubt that a great many men now associated with military matters who are there in perpetuation of the ideas that formerly prevailed, would object to any such proposition. It would introduce a new element into the management of militia affairs; but I urge upon the minister that, the conditions having changed, the old system is no longer suitable and that the change of conditions should be met even by such a conservative institution as the Militia Department of Canada.
What is true in regard to the officers is also true in regard to the men. I am glad to know that the pay of the men has been increased. Judged by military standards generally it is liberal pay, but at the same time it is not liberal pay when judged according to the standard of earnings by men whom it is desirable to get into these militia camps and to have
identified themselves with volunteer affairs. We want to get good men into the volunteer force. We want to get the man who has employment, not the man who has not employment. While a dollar a day and rations may be a reasonable amount to the man who has not employment, it is not reasonable pay to the man who has employment and it is the man who has employment who is the valuable man in a militia camp. While it would be a very radical departure-and I hesitate to make the suggestion, if they were paid just double to_ start with-it would not be more than fair, and I thoroughly believe that if the pay were doubled we would be able to get the class of men to enter the militia force and to take an interest in it who do not do so now. It is not because of the actual cash value, but because they would feel that their willingness to serve their country was being reasonably recognized by the country. At the present time I am satisfied that no man who is in valuable employment can leave that employment and take the risks, which attach to leaving it, who will go to a military camp and serve for a dollar a day and consider that the country is giving him fair and reasonable remuneration for the sacrifice he is making.
I am given to understand that it is difficult to fill the regiments for the annual drill, and that sometimes it is a question of drumming up men who happen not to be in employment at the time in order to fill the regiments at the camp. That is not satisfactory. Instead of being a saving of money, to my mind, it is very largely throwing it away, because you are not "getting the men who, having had training this year, wilL attend the camp next year, and thus have the advantage of the previous training. This country is different from what it used to be, and, different from other countries. We will have to revise our ideas in regard to the volunteer militia if we are going to get the sacrifice and service that we want, and that we were able to get thirty or forty years ago. Our young men have just as much of the spirit of patriotism as the men in those days had, but the conditions are different, and the changed conditions have not been met by a change of conditions in the militia organization.
The low pay which is given to the * men works back on the officers. They must make sacrifices or expenditures in order to keep up the interest of the men. That is an unjust tax upon the officers. It is a principle that is contrary to the spirit of this country, and there should be in substantial and tangible form recognition by the country at large of the sacrifices that are being made for the country by the men who are engaged in the militia force. That would be an inspiration to the force, and would make it an object of ambition instead of

having it looked upon coolly. We hold, too much to the old traditions in regard to militia matters, and are not adapting our militia arrangements to the new conditions.
It may be said that the suggestions I have made would increase the militia expenditure so enormously that they are not to be considered. In my judgment, it would be better to cut the force in half, to have the men _ efficient, enthusiastic, satisfied and ambitious in their calling, than to have the number we have at present with a rather cool and careless spirit. I know the suggestions I have made are very radical, and I quite recognize the courage that^ would be necessary on the part of the minister to accept any of them, but as a rank outsider, as one who has no interest to serve in connection with the militia, but the desire, as an ordinary citizen, to see it efficient to the last degree, creditable to the country, and satisfactory to the men who are in it, I make the suggestions.

Can the minister favour us with some information as to the location of the proposed military school or armoury in Montreal? I understand that he had some interviews with the city council of Montreal as to the location of the drill ground or camp. Can he tell us what conclusion he has arrived at?

The hon. member for
Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has pleaded that he has had no military training. He has certainly the proper military spirit, and if he had just a little bit of training, he would have made an excellent soldier. It is not too late yet, and I would like to see him at the head of one of the squadrons in the Northwest in the near future. I would like to see him in the saddle leading his men into camp. He has referred to the matter of uniforms. I agree with him, and I think everyone will agree, that an officer on becoming qualified should be given his drill uniform, at any rate. 1 do not think there is any reason why an officer should be called upon to put his hand in his pocket and buy the uniform which is necessary for his drill in connection with serving his country in camp, in the cities in evenings on parade. I think .that should be furnished him. The matter is now before a committee of officers to devise the best means of carrying out that suggestion. My hon. friend has spoken about higher pay for the men. What he has said is logically correct, but I do not think that five per cent of the volunteers in Canada go into it for the money. In the city corps they pool the money, they never get it. The same thing holds good with respect to many of the rural corps. In my own old regiment we nearly always paid out more than was paid in. I find it is a question of training. If you give the Mr. OLIVER.
men proper training they will not mind so much what the pay is. It is tha/t spirit that keeps up the regiment. I was in Hamilton not long since, and there were 91 gentlemen sitting at a table. These_ 91 gentlemen had been officers in the service, and I would challenge any one in that city to pick out 91 other men who could equal them. It does not hold good to say that the militia force is made up of the offscourings of the country.

I hope my hon. friend
did not understand me as saying that.

No. Of course, there are men in the regiments who should not be there, but the militiamen of this country will stand second to no other class of men that you can pick out in Canada or anywhere else. As far as the question of my hon. friend from Laval is concerned, I would say that the property known as the Logan farm was handed over to the Dominion Government by tllie Imperial authorities, and in case it was disposed of the proceeds were to go to the Militia Department. In 1908 44 acres, plus, were handed over in fee simple to Montreal for nothing; 31 acres, plus, were handed over to the city of Montreal for ninety-nine years at the nominal rental of one dollar per year, and 3.86 acres were retained by the Militia Department only out of the whole area whereon to erect an ordnance building, or any other building, for the purpose of the Militia Department. A little strip in a square, about 3 acres, or a little less, was being unloaded on the city of Montreal by gentlemen who were interested in the sale of it. I was informed both by the Mayor and an hon. member for that city, a member of the city council, and of this House, that these gentlemen would hand that over for $750,000 to the city of Montreal, provided I, as Minister of Militia, or the Dominion Government, would hand over the balance of the militia property, consisting of 3.86 acres, under the guarantee that we would never build upon it, so that there would be a complete square. I came to the conclusion that the city of Montreal had been fairly well treated by the Militia Department. Taking that valuation of $750,000 for this little corner, the 44 acres are worth from $12,000,000 to $15,000,000, the 31 acres about $9,000,000, and the 3.86 acres $1,000,000. I had no authority, and I did not see that the Government had any authority, to hand over free to any person property which was entrusted to them for militia purposes. It should be used for the development and upkeep of the militia of the country. I declined to hand that 3.86 acres over to the city of Montreal, and, while it is absolutely unsuitable for an ordnance stores building, it would be most admirably suit-

ed for a nice drill hall for one of the new regiments. The 85th, a- French regiment, is growing up in that part of the city. It will likely become a city regiment soon, and it is quite possible the department may see its way clear to erecting a drill hall on that site and thus save possibly three quarters of a million which would have to be spent in buying a site for a drill hall. I might add that St. Helen's island, an historic property, was also handed over to the city of Montreal for $200,000. These properties, it has been estimated are to-day worth $47,000,000 that the Militia Department might have had if they had not been handed over as I have indicated.

I do not think'
the minister has answered my question. I *want to know whether the minister has come to any decision with Tegard to the building of a military school.
A military school is going to be built at Dorval.
If there is one built at Dorval there will not be one built in the city?
No, there will be a drill hall.

Where is the property
situated in Dorval?
It is the old race course.
The uniform will be for active service.

Yes, but we are not on active service all the time. You have to appeal to the vanity of the men and the vanity of the officers, and that vanity is a laudable ambition to make a creditable display. What makes a corps efficient? It is in the vanity or the ambition of the officers and men to make that corps better

than any other corps. As we. all know, the backbone of the militia, outside of the officers, are the non-commissioned officers, and my idea about pay is: the ordinary man in the militia gets enough pay; some of them are not woTth the pay they receive and a great many of them ought never be brought into camp. On the other hand, a great many of the men are efficient, and will make splendid soldiers. We have started under the late Minister of Militia with efficiency pay, when a man reaches a certain qualification. In order to have good non-commissioned officers, I would give him, when he has passed an examination showing his efficiency to command and thoroughly instruct a squad, not only a bonus for qualifying and spending the time required for study for that examination, but after he passes the examination and shows himself efficient as an instructor, I would in addition to the bonus, give him increased pay. For men who are not efficient the pay is wasted on them. But to the man who can pass an examination and qualify as a rifle shot, I would give more pay. To the -non-commissioned officer who could qualify as a squad instructor, J_ would pay a decent, respectable wage. I appeal to the Minister of Militia, if he wants to gain the gratitude of the officers of the Canadian militia, to abolish the duty on officers' uniforms.

I am sorry I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Sunbury and Queens (Mr. McLean) in everything he has stated, although he is a thorough soldier and a good officer and knows what he is talking about. There is no doubt that very many of the men taken to camp are useless and the money spent on them is squandered, but I am afraid my hon. friend is not taking the right way to remedy that. Possibly I have too low an idea of the object of the militia to rise to the standard	the Minister of
Militia sets before him, but I have always tried to look upon the militia as a business proposition. The only justification for spending any money on the militia is that some portion of our population should always have some grounding in the rudiments of military training, so that we may have men in Canada, not necessarily in the active militia, who in case of trouble would be something like the reserves in Europe, and who could be brought into line within a reasonable time. That was illustrated in the South African War. The minister, who was there, will I think agree with me that the men who had some previous military training got into the idea of their duties much quicker than the men who had not. The next idea I have is that you should teach the men to shoot, because if a man cannot Mr. McLEAN (Sunbury and Queens).
handle a rifle he is no good in the militia. You ought to Lave in the militia, not the offscourings of the earth, but the very best class of men in Canada, and you cannot get that class without paying them. I am assuming that you can get a better class of men in the cities for a small amount of money than you can get in the country districts because the city men go to the drill hall in the evening, they pool their money, they take some amusement out of it, and they do not have to give up theii ordinary avocations of life as has the man in the rural districts when he, goes to camp and leaves the work on his farm. The industrious man who has work to do is the only man worth training. Then, in my judgment, the minister is spending too much money on fluff and feathers and not enough on the real backbone of the organization. According to the departmental report, the expenditure for the annual drill in 1911 was $1,159,000 of which only $750,000 went to pay and allowances for the officers and men. That is, hardly two-thirds of the total outlay goes to the actual payment of the officer and men. It is true there was some Slight increase last year. I understand the minister now pays the ordinary man a dollar a day. Before that he got fifty cents a clay and his efficiency pay, which brought, it up to about 90 cents. I think it would have been very much better to have increased the pay of the man and not the horse. My experience is that I never had any difficulty in getting horses. I could have Tecruited horses for half a dozen batteries every year at a dollar a day without any trouble. In the, country regiments there is no trouble whatever in getting horses, the trouble is to get men. Many officers in Canada make the horses bring the men; that is, no man can get a horse on unless he brings a man with it. If you double the pay of the men, you will only add at the outside three-quarters of a million dollars, which is a mere bagatelle to my hon. friend. He should pay the men $2 a day, if necessary, and get the very -best men he can. These men do not stay in the militia very long as a rule. They bind themselves for three years; but the rule is not enforced. On an average they do not get more than three or four years training, and the training which they do get is very rudimentary indeed. If you increase the pay and get the best men, you will be giving them some start along militia training; and, if the time should ever come when their services are required, they would be ready to be of some use to the state.

I wish to support what my hon. friend the member for Queens and Sun-bury (Mr. McLean) said about the

uniforms. I think no customs duties should
be levied upon the uniforms of our officers and soldiers. The same thing might be said about the minister's uniforms. A Minister has to wear first-class and second-class uniforms and has to pay duty on them.
It is unfair that a minister of the Crown should pay duty on his uniforms. The officers in our militia should not be called upon to pay duty on their uniforms. The question has come up here before and I do not know what excuse has been given.
I would ask my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Eeid) to remove the duty and save this expense to the officers who give their time and their money for the sake of the militia and for the defence of the country,

It is the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) who
makes the tariff; I only administer it.

Yes, but surely the hon. gentleman 'has some influence over the Minister of Finance, who is only a newcomer, who is only a convert of the last minute to the great Conservative party. My hon. friend ought to tell him that it is in the spirit of the Conservative party to treat the officers fairly.
I agree with you.

My hon. friend from
Laval (Mir. Wilson) has raised a very interesting question in regard to the city of Montreal. I agree entirely with the hon. Minister of Militia that the city of Montreal has been royally treated by the Government of Canada. The Logan farm, or the Lafontaine farm as it is known to-day in the east, an'd St. Helen's Island were practically given over to the city of Montreal. I hope that the city authorities of Montreal will understand that the Government should have their say in the matter of the proposed alienation of such properties. At all events, no land speculation should be allowed with regard to that very valuable strip of land. It is the property of the Government and it should be enjoyed by the people of Montreal. It is a splendid park in the very heart of _ the city. The Minister of Militia should utilize that park for drills, parades and military exercises. I do not think, however that he should erect buildings on that property. There is already one building there, the Normal School, and for many years I have heard some people connected with the municipality of Montreal state that the time might come when this,would be removed. If an armoury is erected, it should be a building that will appeal to the artistic sense of the people.
During the session I had the pleasure of receiving the report of my hon. friend the
Minister of Militia in regard to his trip to England and France to which he referred a moment ago. He followed the manoeuvres in England and was allowed to follow the manoeuvres in France. Will he tell me how many officers and men accompanied him in England and France, and what is the cost, in total, of that expeditionary force?

Colonel Hodgins, Colonel Landry, Colonel Maunsell, Colonel Morrison and Major Roberston in Engand, five I think. In France, Colonel Landry, and Major Robertson. As to the total cost, I have not the figures here, but I think it is only $4,000.
For all?
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Sun-bury and Queens state that all the militia officers had to take a course of instruction. I would like to know if that is a general provision. I know it is not the case in the country from which I come. Many hold positions in the western country who never had any military training and never went to a school of instruction. I am aware it is not so all over Canada, but I would like to know from the minister if qualification is necessary for an applicant for a commission in the militia,

Every officer has to qualify. Of course, he may be appointed provisionally, but he is supposed to qualify within a year. If the hon. gentleman will look through the militia list, he will find that the great majority of the corps in the West have officers who are qualified. Some of the mounted corps in the West have every officer qualified. Some of the squadrons in the North have officers who have not had opportunity to attend schools. They are supposed to qualify within a year of appointment, or the time may >be extended if necessary.
Mr. White (Victoria, Alta.) : The mounted infantry established some years ago- the Alberta Mounted Rifles-have no qualified officers in the three companies of the corps. Take the corp at Fort Saskatchewan, they also have some officers without qualification.

If the hon. gentleman
will look at the militia list, he will find that the 15th of Calgary has every officer qualified, except some of the second lieutenants. The corps to which he refers, I believe, the 19th Dragoons. It has many qualified officers. The second lieutenants who are recently appointed have not qualified, but they will do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before whom do they qualify, before a board?
Yes, they have to go to a school of instruction, or to the board. We will mail to my hon. friend a statement of how to -qualify.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Listening to	the addresses of	the hon.
member for Edmonton and others, I noted the questions as to why we were not able to get the best men. One reason, I think, is this point I have referred to-that the -officers are not qualified. With the short time allowed for -drill and with unqualified officers, the young man who might volunteer is led to think he could not be taught even ordinary drill. So, they cannot be expected to take much interest in the matter. There is another reason. I quite agree with the minister that it is not for the money, and yet there must be some inducement for the kind of man the minister desires to obtain, these young farmers and those who bring their own horses if possible, and who would be there year after year and -would become proficient in three years. I have made many inquiries among the young men as to why they did not enlist, and generally their answer was that there was no inducement^ One cause is -that there is no rifle range in the country. If they had an opportunity of using a range and learning to shoot there would be some inducement and many more would volunteer. It seems to me that it is not enough merely to go to Calgary for a few days in the year. Many of these young men have told me that they have never fired a rifle, and yet they are drawing money as having trained in rifle practice. I know as a matter of fact that they get no rifle practice at their headquarters, and if they get any at all it must be at brigade camp 'in Calgary. I should think the money spent to acquire ranges would be well spent. A few years ago, the -major in command of the company at Fort Saskatchewan took the trouble to come to Ottawa to induce the department to purchase a range that had many natural advantages-a natural cut bank on the river of seventy-five feet, a place which had advantages over almost any other that could be chosen. The department did not take the matter up at the time. But I think if the minister would spend some money in securing ranges it would not be a difficult thing to get young men to volunteer. And I -believe, as has been said, that the inducement would be greater than double pay.

We are encouraging the use of rifle ranges, but it takes time and money. We -are establishing miniature ranges in many places, but I will not take up time with that.. I agTee with a great deal of what the hon. gentleman has said.
Mr. WHITE (Victoria, Alta.).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A few years ago rifle clubs were formed, as I understand it, under the department. Not only militiamen, but civilians joined. But afterwards that was done away with. I think the movement was a good one, and that it was unfortunate that it was stopped. It would teach many men to shoot.

They are still open to
be formed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But there are no ranges. I think we had about seventy members in Fort Saskatchewan, but when the rifle range was taken away-it was in connection with that that the major came to Ottawa-the club did not succeed.

We vote ranges every
year in different parts of the country, but it takes a lot of time and money.
82 cadets corps, $325,000.

Would the minister give
some account of the constitution and purpose of these cadet corps?

These young men train
without any pay as boys. The formation of these corps is based on the principle that when the mind is young and the body is young is the time to mould those minds and bodies. We aim to establish a cadet corps on a good basis in the hope that these young men will learn to drill when they are young and thus naturally take to militia work, just as they would take to any other training before becoming set in their ways. Members may see the cadet corps in almost any portion of Canada. I reviewed four thousand from the French colleges in Montreal a week ago and nearly four thousand in Toronto last Saturday.

They are in connection
with schools, are they not?

Largely in connection
with schools as yet, but they are also in connection with the regiments. Nearly every company is now getting its cadet corps as a feeder, so to speak. They are splendidly drilled fellows. I noticed two or three corps, one from St. Catharines, and I venture to say that half of the young men in those corps could pass their examinations for officers' certificates. I was amazed! at their proficiency. It is marvellous the way the young men are taking part in this work. Anyone at the Toronto exhibition last year who saw the mounted cadet corps from the West will admit that they were the chief attraction of the fair, and nothing could exceed the manner in which they handled their horses. They get one dollar a year towards uniforms besides their transportation and board while in camp. There are about 35,000 of them, 15,000 in the province of Quebec; 6,000 in and

around Montreal alone. At the Mount St. Louis institution they had 600 on parade the o'ther day, a splendid battalion of as fine looking boys as you could find in Canada. The movement is spreading and in that way I hope that in the course of a few years, these young men will- work into the militia force of the country; and while I do not care to say what I intend to do I have plans made whereby the whole force, in the course of a few years, may be considerably modified and changed. It is found that this training has a splendid tendency to keep them right. People all over the country of all classes are taking hold of it. They see the benefit of-it. It is controlled play. That is one reason why I want the drill halls all over the country; it gives the boys a chance to get in and drill instead of being on the streets. It is controlled play instead of uncontrolled play. We 'train them also in the same way as the scouts are trained, in camp. Many gentlemen hesitated about allowing their sons to go into these corps last year. We trained 8,000. One head of a collegiate institute went with his son and he is now one of tire most enthusiastic advocates of this system in Canada. It is found that the whole surroundings are favourable and the tendency is to build up the manhood of the boys.
Wliat is the money for?

There are cadet organizers in each division all over Canada. They go around to tire various localities in the country and organize the boys into squadrons and start them drilling. There are transport and travelling and subsistence of these officers, $11,000. Then there are nineteen instructors of the permanent force, $1,900. They get a temporary payment of $100 each. Then there is subsistence, $10,000. . We are taking school teachers into camp for training in connection with the cadets. This year it is estimated that one thousand school teachers are taking the course, at a cost of $75,000. Besides that there is the transport of
30,000	cadets, and things like that.

Are arms furnished to
them?

We have not furnished
arms except the regular rifles in some cases for shooting. We are now getting a cheap cadet rifle, not an inferior rifle, and now we give a few of those for shooting purposes. We do not pretend to arm them all with rifles, that would cost too much money.
How much of the Strathccna fund is spent on that account?

The Strathcona fund is
not applied to this account, but _ to the physical training in connection with the schools of the provinces.

I am a peaceful man
myself, but still I have had some experience in my own family, but I am prepared to testify that the training the boys get in these cadet corps is a mighty good thing for the boys, even if they should never have to defend their homes. I am speaking from experience. My son who went through the cadet corps became a captain in his regiment before he died.
A fine boy, too.

He took his examination in Toronto. I never begrudged the money it cost because it developed him physically to start with. He was not what you would call a robust looking boy at first, but after the training in the cadet corps, he developed into a very strong man. I am in favour of that training if there never were any war like attitude to it at all on account of the improvement it makes in many ways. As to the regiment life in the armoury, I think it is a very good thing for the young men even when they get into that. I speak from experience from the Brockville regiment. The members of that regiment spend a great many of their evenings at the armoury, they have their indoor baseball and such games organized among themselves and make it a source of entertainment to themselves and to others; they are improving themselves, and while they are there we know where they are. At the same time they are being developed physically.
A word about the efficiency of some of the boys in these corps. An inspecting officer came to Brdckville at one time and we had a cadet corps under a young man name Murray. The inspecting officer told me that there was only one captain in the regiment who was superior to this boy in the handling of his company, and an outsider watching would doubt that. I watched this young boy putting his company through their manoeuvres, and I thought he was quite as efficient as any officer of the regiment. The inspecting officer told me that if he had to award a prize there was only one commanding officer in the whole regiment whom he would think superior to this young man. I am not opposed to anything that trains our young men, to make better men of them. I do not mean to say that I am a militarist-I believe there is reason in these things-but I want to say a word in favour of the training of the boys as cadets outside of the militia altogether. It helps them physically, morally and in every other way so long as it is properly done.

What is the age of the
cadets?	1

From twelve to eighteen, when they can enter the militia.
Clothing, $700,000.
I understood the minister to say that there were only two Highland regiments in the province of Nova Scotia, the 78th and the 94th.

I think there is only
one with the Highland uniform, the 78th. Has the 94th the Highland uniform?

No, but they are very anxious to get it, and they would like the minister to help them. They are a much older regiment than the 78th. I think it is the oldest Highland regiment in the province of Nova Scotia.

Inasmuch as my hon.
friend bears a Highland name, he might visit the department and talk the matter over with another Highlander, Quartermaster General McDonald. They might come to an agreement.

What is the position of
the department in regard to uniforms? I notice they are of very great variety.

It is usually left to each corps to decide. The Moosejaw regiment want the rifle uniform, and you cannot coax some other regiments to have it. Cavalry regiments want the scarlet. The Regina regiment want the rifle uniform, while Saskatoon regiment insist on the scarlet, as does also the Prince Albert regiment. We do not interfere in the matter specially.

Is it not now accepted
by military authorities the world over that khaki or a similar colour is the better colour?	_
That is for drill purposes. All the city corps are getting the khaki uniform now, but they usually have other uniforms for state occasions.

If this force is actually
for fighting purposes, and if the proper uniform to fight in is grey or a dun colour, does the department not provide all with that uniform, whether in city or country?

If the country regiments want it, we give it, instead of the scarlet or any other colour. The country regiments going into camp get overalls, but most of them prefer to have a scarlet or rifle uniform in addition to the drill uniform.	.

I think if this force is
for a certain ultimate purpose, the uniform should not be a matter of choice, it should be a matter of policy of the Government. The regiments should be fitted with arms and uniforms that have been found by the latest experience to be the most efficient and desirable.
Mr. OLIVER.
Contingencies, $44,000.

Might I make a suggestion. I think we have discussed pretty well nearly all the items, but I understand that some hon. gentlemen want to make some further remarks. Suppose we put all these Items through, but reserve item 90, and hon. gentlemen who wants to discuss these matters further can do so on this item.

I am agreeable to anything. I want to thank the House for the very fair and open discussion we have had. I am more than pleased with the interest that is 'being taken by members representing the people in the perfection of the Militia Department. Let me say, as most hon. gentlemen who have taken part in the discussion know, that not only in this House, but personally, I am always pleased to receive any suggestion for the upbuilding of the force. Whatever others may do, I regard this as an absolutely non-political department, and I want hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House to feel that I am open to suggestions. My hon. friend mentioned that an officer had written to him. A man does not lose his rights by becoming a member of the militia force, and he is at perfect liberty to write to his member of Parliament, or to the Minister of Militia, and tell him what he thinks of him.

I would like the minister to pay my man for his horse, then.
Progress reported.

I have the honour to inform the House that I have received from James J. Donnelly, Esquire, his resignation as member for the electoral district of South Bruce, in the province of Ontario. I have in consequence issued my warrant to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to make out a new writ of election for the said electoral district.
